articles.full_text:
NATO fighter jets were scrambled in Lithuania after a suspected drone crossed into the country, forcing Vilnius Airport in the capital to close its airspace. Lithuanian authorities issued a possible air threat alert to residents, urging them to find a safe place.
The suspected drone was detected entering Lithuania's airspace from Belarus on Saturday morning, triggering the alarm to be sounded shortly before 10am local time. However, about 40 minutes later, the alert was cancelled as officials said it no longer caused a threat. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Centre, said the object had moved away from the NATO ally's observation zone.
Speaking to public broadcaster LRT TELEVISION, Mr Vitkauskas confirmed a search was underway for the unidentified object. "If it fell, if it was a drone, it will have to be found," he is translated as saying.
"But it couldn't necessarily have been a drone, because certain parameters said that the speed was slightly lower than usual. There could have been some anomaly or it could have been related to bird migration."The senior official previously said the scrambled fighter jets were attempting to confirm the nature of the object which had not been "fully identified".
He earlier said it resembled a drone on radar, but admitted it could have also been a flock of birds. Last month, an Italian figher jet stationed in Lithuania was scrambled after a possible drone sighting which turned out to be birds.
Mr Vitkauskas said authorities received reports from residents of a "possible object outside the territory of Vilnius, moving towards Jonava". Lithuania, along with its Baltic neighbours, have faced repeated drone incursions since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The number of incidents have risen in recent months as countries along NATO's eastern flank warn of an increasing threat from Moscow. In September, an Italian fighter jet shot down a suspsected drone over Lithuania. It resembled the first time a UAV had been shot down in the country's airspace.
The Italian air force has been stationed at Šiauliai Air Base, northern Lithuania, as part of the NATO Air Defence mission. NATO nations strengthen alliance airspace along its eastern flank on a four-month rotation.
Lithuania has a southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key ally of Russia, while also having a border with Kaliningrad - Russia's heavily militarised Baltic exclave. The suspected drone incursion comes as Lithuania holds its largests annual national mobilisation exercise, testing how it would react in a crisis.
Some 3,000 officials, as well as 1,000 volunteers, are taking part in Vyio Skliautas 2026 which ends on Saturday. The major drills include rehearsing for the evacuation of residents.
Vilnius is drawing up evacuation plans with neighbouring Poland in the event of an attack by Russia. The NATO allies are working on a bilateral agreement to provide a framework for the plans amid rising fears of a Russian assault.
Moscow has ramped up its threats this week, directly warning NATO it is ready to use its "entire arsenal" if the alliance threatened Kaliningrad. NATO condemned Russia for "irresponsible nuclear rhetoric".

articles.title: China Launches Anti-Dumping Probe Into EU Chemical Imports Days Before Crucial Beijing Trade Talks – Another Tit-for-Tat Escalation That Could Hit Your Wallet - USA Herald
articles.summary: China Launches Anti-Dumping Probe Into EU Chemical Imports Days Before Crucial Beijing Trade Talks – Another Tit-for-Tat Escalation That Could Hit Your Wallet  USA Herald
articles.full_text:
BEIJING — China has opened a new anti-dumping investigation into European chemical imports just days before a high-stakes round of trade talks with Brussels, a timing that analysts see as a deliberate show of leverage. The commerce ministry announced the probe on October 3, targeting a widely used industrial chemical, and the move adds another chapter to a trade fight that has already touched electric vehicles, pork, and now plastics.
The Target: P-Nitrotoluene
The investigation focuses on p-nitrotoluene, an industrial chemical used in the manufacture of dyes, pharmaceuticals, and pesticides. China's commerce ministry said domestic producers had raised concerns about "damage to production and operations" caused by low-priced imports from the European Union.
Under Chinese trade rules, the probe is expected to conclude within 12 months, with the option of a six-month extension. During that time, Beijing can impose provisional duties if investigators find evidence of dumping, a tool China has used in earlier disputes with European exporters.
Talks Loom Between Brussels and Beijing
The timing is hard to miss. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao are scheduled to hold critical discussions in the days ahead. Investigations like this one are widely read as bargaining chips: they put pressure on the other side while costing the initiator little in the short term.
A ministry spokesperson framed the matter as Europe's responsibility. "China has repeatedly reiterated that the EU needs to face its own economic and trade problems directly and resolve mutual concerns through dialogue and consultation," the spokesperson said.
A Tit-for-Tat Pattern
The new probe follows a familiar rhythm. In September, the European Union began investigating polyvinyl chloride imports from China and other countries, and Beijing signaled countermeasures. The EU has argued that Chinese exports benefit from extensive state subsidies that distort global markets. China rejects that claim and has repeatedly threatened retaliation against what it calls European protectionism.
The pattern is not new. In recent years Beijing has launched trade probes into European products after Brussels moved against Chinese goods, including investigations tied to the dispute over electric vehicle tariffs. Each round has raised the stakes for exporters on both sides and unsettled global supply chains.
Why Americans Should Pay Attention
It may look like a distant dispute over an obscure chemical, but the consequences travel. Chemicals like p-nitrotoluene sit near the start of long manufacturing chains. Disruptions or duties can ripple into the prices of pharmaceuticals, agricultural products, and industrial goods that eventually reach American shelves.
There is also a strategic dimension. The European Union and China together account for an enormous share of world trade, and a deeper rupture between them would reshape where manufacturers source materials and where exporters redirect goods. When products are shut out of one market, they often flood another, and the United States is frequently that destination. U.S. companies already navigating tariffs and supply chain uncertainty have reason to watch closely.
Washington's own trade posture toward Beijing also makes Europe's choices consequential. How the EU balances protecting its industry against keeping channels open to China will influence how much pressure American officials can expect to share, or be asked to coordinate, in the months ahead.
What to Watch Next
The first signal will be the tone out of the Sefcovic-Wang meeting: whether both sides emerge with a path to de-escalation or with new threats. Analysts will also look at whether Beijing widens the list of targeted European products, and whether Brussels responds with additional investigations of its own.
The anti-dumping case will move slowly, but its political purpose is immediate. By opening it now, China has told European negotiators that it is prepared to answer pressure with pressure. Whether that strengthens its hand at the table, or hardens European resolve, may define the next phase of one of the world's most consequential trade relationships.

articles.title: Second Kyiv bridge hit in two days as Russia targets Dnipro crossings - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Second Kyiv bridge hit in two days as Russia targets Dnipro crossings  Euronews.comRussia hits second major bridge in Ukraine's capital Kyiv  BBCUkraine war briefing: Russian attacks on Kyiv bridges cause traffic chaos  The GuardianRussia strikes another major bridge in Kyiv as attacks on Ukrainian capital escalate  CNNRussia bombs Kyiv bridge in new tactic to carve city in two  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
With the Northern Bridge's traffic blocked a day after jet-powered drones forced the Southern Bridge shut, two of the eight Dnipro crossings joining Kyiv's halves are now disrupted.
A Russian strike hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge on Saturday, halting traffic from the left bank to the right and deepening a transport crisis that began when the Southern Bridge was shut a day earlier.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the strike on Telegram after a drone alert in the capital. "Northern Bridge has been hit," he wrote. "Emergency services are heading to the scene."
He later reported damage to the road surface and to the overhead wires that power trolleybuses on the bridge. "Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.
The strike is the latest in a series aimed at the crossings over the Dnipro, the river that separates Kyiv's eastern and western districts. Eight bridges connect the two sides, and city officials say the campaign is "tearing Kyiv apart".
The Southern Bridge, a cable-stayed span and one of the city's main crossings, was closed on Friday after waves of fast, jet-powered drones struck. Officials said it had been hit several times since Thursday. Movement on another bridge was also restricted.
The closures brought severe congestion across the city. Cars and buses stood in long queues on major roads as drivers looked for other ways across, and some commuters had to finish their journeys on foot.
Klitschko warned on Friday that the capital should now be on a war footing.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war has largely been fought on the ground in the east, and Kyiv has mostly been spared the destruction seen near the front line.

articles.summary: Malta introduces penalty framework for CBAM  Deloitte
articles.full_text:
Deloitte Malta Tax Alert

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) puts a carbon cost on specified goods imported into the EU: cement, iron and steel, aluminium, chemicals, fertilisers, hydrogen and electricity. Since 1 January 2026, certain importers of these goods must, in principle, be or act through an authorised CBAM declarant. They must declare the emissions embedded in their imports each year and surrender CBAM certificates to cover them. The first CBAM declaration and surrender, for imports made during 2026, is due by 30 September 2027. The main highlights are summarised below.
On 25 September 2026, Malta introduced regulations in the form of Legal Notice 254 of 2026 ‘Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Implementing) Regulations, 2026’ (the ‘Regulations’). These Regulations implement the requirements of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (Regulation (EU) 2023/956, the "CBAM Regulation") as regards the imposition and enforcement of administrative penalties.
Framework of penalties
The Regulations provide that any authorised CBAM declarant, importer or authorised representative within the scope of the CBAM Regulation who fails to comply with its provisions may be subject to the measures and administrative penalties set out in Article 16(3) and (4) of Directive 2003/87/EC (which established the EU Emissions Trading System for greenhouse gases), and in regulation 9(7) and (8) of the Maltese rules transposing that Directive (S.L. 643.02).
In summary, under the EU Emissions Trading System, an operator that does not surrender, by 30 September each year, a sufficient number of allowances to cover its emissions for the preceding year is generally liable to an excess emissions penalty of EUR 100 for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) not covered, indexed to the European consumer index. In principle, payment of the penalty would not release the operator from the obligation to surrender the missing allowances.
Imposition of penalties
The Climate Action Authority would notify the authorised CBAM declarant, or the person in breach, in writing of the administrative penalty imposed, by means of a judicial letter. The person notified may appeal within 20 days from the date of service before the Administrative Review Tribunal.
Next steps
Businesses importing goods that are likely to fall within the scope of the CBAM Regulation are strongly advised to consider whether any exemption or threshold could apply, assess whether they need to apply for the status of authorised CBAM declarant, and engage with their suppliers early to obtain the emissions data that may be needed.
How we can help
If you have questions regarding the obligations outlined above and wish to find out more about the impact of the CBAM on your business, please do not hesitate to contact us.

articles.summary: EU pushes Ukraine for further reforms to unlock funding  Financial TimesEurope is losing patience with Ukraine’s demands  UnHerdUkraine's 2026 budget, defence needs are covered, EU says  ReutersUkraine’s war chest is running low at the worst possible moment  politico.euUkraine nets 2.9 billion euros from EU after passing reforms  The Kyiv Independent
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the War in Ukraine myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
Brussels has rebuffed Ukraine’s request for additional financial support this year, demanding that Kyiv implement promised reforms before receiving further EU funding.
The decision comes as Ukraine grapples with intensified Russian attacks on civilian infrastructure, while its parliament struggles to pass the reforms required to unlock support from the EU and other donors.
This summer, Kyiv identified an additional $27bn in military needs and asked the European Commission to help cover the gap by bringing forward tranches from a €90bn EU loan agreed late last year.
That loan was intended to cover most of Ukraine’s financing needs in 2026 and 2027, allocating up to €45bn each year if certain reform milestones were met. However, only €15.7bn of this has been disbursed this year, partly due to delays in complying with reform requirements.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said further funding is urgently needed, in part to boost production of drones and interceptors as Moscow intensifies its aerial attacks on Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure ahead of the winter.
But Brussels rejected the request to frontload 2027 funding, instead pressing Kyiv to meet conditions that could unlock about €34bn in EU support this year.
In a joint statement on Thursday, Ukraine and the European Commission said they had “identified the means to cover Ukraine’s budget and defence needs for 2026. We have also reconfirmed the steps needed to ensure their timely release.”
The reforms Ukraine must deliver to receive the funds include the abolition of a VAT exemption for small parcels and the introduction of new taxation rules for digital platforms.
Both measures have passed in parliament, but include a controversial amendment that weakens the rules governing politically exposed persons (PEPs), which had been requested by the EU to strengthen anti-corruption efforts. That amendment, if signed into law, could threaten Ukraine’s compliance with the conditions attached to EU funding.
European commissioners Valdis Dombrovskis and Marta Kos wrote a letter to the Speaker of Ukraine’s parliament, underscoring that additional financial assistance in 2026 was still available to Ukraine if it fulfilled the requested reforms.
“Avoiding any weakening of Ukraine’s framework on PEPs” was “essential”, they wrote in the letter, which was seen by the FT.
In an interview with the FT on Thursday, Zelenskyy pushed back against media reports of tense discussions with Commission president Ursula von der Leyen over reform conditions.
“We had a very good meeting with Ursula and with her team, and she understands that they have to help Ukraine,” he said.
Europe should help close Kyiv’s financing gap “because we are defending them”, he added. “They have to do it for them also, not only for us.”
He said he had told von der Leyen that wartime pressures meant reforms could not always proceed according to a normal timetable.
“We have to defend [ourselves] now, and some decisions, financial decisions, you can’t wait ,” he said. “Because it’s a question of our stability.”
The Commission is also assessing Ukraine’s yet-uncovered financing needs for 2027, which officials said could total about €70bn in military and budgetary support. The assessment is expected to be presented to EU leaders meeting in mid-October.
Ukraine is in discussions with the IMF about further disbursements from its $8bn programme, a review of which is due later this year. Those disbursements are contingent on funding agreements from the EU and Kyiv’s other allies that will help cover Ukraine’s financial needs in 2027.

French government bond yields climbed to a fresh 18-year high after recording their biggest quarterly increase in nearly four decades, highlighting growing investor concerns over the country's fiscal position.
According to Reuters, markets have increasingly priced in higher borrowing costs as rising energy prices threaten to keep inflationary pressures elevated, raising concerns about debt affordability in heavily indebted euro zone economies such as France and Italy.

Germany's benchmark 10-year Bund yield was up 1 basis point on Thursday. It had reached 3.6526% on Monday, its highest level since June 2009, and ended the third quarter around 71 basis points higher.

Money markets were pricing the ECB's deposit rate at around 2.81% by December, implying one 25-basis-point rate increase and assigning a 24% probability to a second move. Markets also priced the policy rate at around 3.42% by late 2027, compared with the current 2.50%.
Higher borrowing costs have renewed scrutiny of fiscal sustainability across the euro zone, particularly in countries carrying large debt burdens. Political uncertainty ahead of elections in 2027 has added to concerns about the trajectory of public finances in France and Italy.
The spread between French and German 10-year government bond yields, a key measure of the premium investors demand to hold French debt, stood at 127.51 basis points. It had widened to 128.80 basis points earlier, its highest level since June 2012.
Italy's 10-year yield spread over German Bunds also widened to 104.15 basis points, its highest level since June 2025, underscoring the broader pressure on eurozone government debt markets as investors reassess the outlook for inflation, interest rates and public finances, according to Reuters.

articles.title: Why the EU's sanctions on Sudan's gold trade are fundamentally flawed - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Why the EU's sanctions on Sudan's gold trade are fundamentally flawed  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
For more than three years, Sudan has been trapped in a war that has shattered cities, emptied villages and pushed millions into displacement. Since fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in 2023, international diplomacy produced no shortage of conferences, ceasefire proposals and mediation initiatives.
Yet each new round of negotiations has been overtaken by renewed violence on the ground. The human cost has continued to rise, with more than 150,000 people estimated dead, over 14 million displaced, and famine spreading across parts of Sudan.
Against this backdrop, the EU has increasingly turned to sanctions as its principal instrument of engagement. Its latest package, adopted in July 2026, represents a notable shift. Rather than expanding the practice of blacklisting individuals and companies, Brussels moved to target Sudan's war economy, banning imports of Sudanese gold and prohibiting exports of mercury and cyanide used in gold extraction.
The change is significant, but raises a larger question. Can economic sanctions succeed when they target the commodity that finances the war while leaving intact the regional networks making that trade profitable?
The EU is not new to sanctions against Sudan. It has maintained an arms embargo since the mid-1990s, later incorporating its measures into the UN sanctions regime on Darfur. In October 2023, Brussels established a dedicated sanctions framework against individuals and entities deemed responsible for undermining Sudan's stability. Over the following two years, the list expanded to include military commanders, financial institutions, and companies linked to SAF and the RSF.
These measures carried political symbolism, not leverage. Most sanctioned actors possessed few assets within European jurisdictions, while the financial foundations of the conflict remained intact.
Gold smuggling, illicit arms transfers, and cross-border financial networks continued to generate resources keeping the warfare financed. As long as these revenue streams remained intact, neither side faced meaningful economic pressure to compromise.
Targeting gold
The July 2026 sanctions package therefore reflects an important strategic adjustment. Instead of targeting the people who profit from war, the EU is attempting to constrain the commodity that finances much of it.
The timing was hardly accidental. Only days earlier, the European Parliament had overwhelmingly voted to call for the RSF to be designated a terrorist organisation following escalating atrocities, particularly the siege of el-Obeid, where hundreds of thousands of civilians remain trapped.
Gold has become the country's most valuable export and one of the conflict's principal financial lifelines
Yet the Council of the EU chose a different course. Rather than adopting the Parliament's recommendation, it focused on restricting Sudanese gold exports and limiting access to mining chemicals.
This distinction matters. It suggests that Brussels is more comfortable regulating trade than confronting the political and diplomatic ramifications of directly escalating pressure on the actors and states enabling Sudan's war.
Targeting gold reflects an accurate diagnosis of Sudan's political economy. Gold has become the country's most valuable export and one of the conflict's principal financial lifelines. It is estimated that between half and three-quarters of Sudan's annual gold production leaves the country through smuggling networks before entering international markets.
The problem is that gold is uniquely difficult to sanction.
Unlike oil or agricultural commodities, refined gold carries no identifiable origin. Once processed by an accredited refinery, Sudanese bullion becomes chemically indistinguishable from gold mined anywhere else. Documentation can be altered, certificates of origin can be recreated, and shipments can be routed through intermediary trading hubs before entering global markets. By the time refined gold reaches Europe, tracing its true origin becomes extraordinarily difficult.
Without internationally coordinated traceability standards extending beyond European borders, banning direct imports of Sudanese gold risks closing only one of many available routes. Much of the trade can simply continue through neighbouring jurisdictions and international refining centres before quietly re-entering formal markets.
The second pillar of the package faces similar constraints. The EU has prohibited exports of mercury and cyanide, essential chemicals used in industrial gold extraction. While this addresses a genuine component of Sudan's mining sector, Europe is not the dominant supplier of these materials.
Alternative sources in Russia, China, and regional trading hubs remain available outside EU jurisdiction. Unless other major exporters adopt comparable restrictions, the sanctions are unlikely to create a decisive shortage.
Precious mettle
Perhaps the greatest weakness, however, lies elsewhere. The package concentrates on regulating trade while largely avoiding the financial and logistical networks that sustain it. Smuggled gold does not move through anonymous markets.
It travels through identifiable intermediaries, financial institutions, transport companies, and commercial partners operating across the region. Likewise, weapons, financing and foreign fighters continue to reach Sudan through external channels despite existing embargoes.
Sanctioning gold while leaving much of the commodity’s infrastructure facilitating its movement intact, risks treating the symptoms of Sudan's war economy rather than its architecture. It closes the main gate while keeping the side doors unlocked.
Sudan's conflict cannot be labelled simply as a civil war. It has evolved into a struggle between rival centres of military power sustained by extensive regional support networks. Both the SAF and the RSF have benefited, in different ways, from external political backing, financial assistance and military cooperation since the conflict began.
This reality fundamentally shapes the effectiveness of sanctions.
The RSF's ability to finance military operations depends less on direct access to European markets than on its capacity to monetise gold through regional intermediaries before those resources enter the wider global economy.
Similarly, the SAF continues to draw upon external partnerships that extend well beyond Sudan's borders. As long as these broader networks remain largely insulated from European pressure, restrictions imposed solely within the EU will have only limited influence over battlefield dynamics.
A significant gap has emerged between the European Parliament and the Council. In its July 2026 resolution, the Parliament departed from previous diplomatic caution by explicitly naming foreign actors accused of supporting the RSF, reflecting growing evidence from international investigations and human rights organisations.
The Council, however, stopped short of turning this political stance into binding sanctions.
Limits of statecraft
This divergence exposes the limits of European economic statecraft. Restricting gold imports or mining chemical exports carries limited political costs for Brussels.
By contrast, sanctioning foreign sponsors, financial facilitators, or commercial intermediaries would be more contentious, risking wider diplomatic and economic repercussions beyond Sudan.
That does not render the July sanctions insignificant. Stricter compliance rules, stronger due diligence for gold traders, and higher reputational risks for refiners can raise the cost of illicit trade, disrupt financial networks and gradually reduce opportunities for conflict financing.
Sudan's experience since 2023 suggests that sanctions succeed only when they target the complete ecosystem sustaining armed violence rather than isolated components of it.
As long as gold can be laundered through intermediary markets, mining inputs sourced elsewhere, and external networks continue providing finance and military assistance, the economic foundations of the conflict will remain largely untouched.
The EU has undeniably introduced new friction into Sudan's wartime economy. Yet friction is not the same as disruption.
Whether this latest sanctions package marks a genuine turning point will ultimately depend not on the regulation of commodities, but on whether Brussels is prepared to confront the wider regional networks that continue to make Sudan's war both affordable and sustainable.

articles.title: France debt crisis: Investors render a ‘guilty’ verdict and are pricing in growing odds of default - Fortune
articles.summary: France debt crisis: Investors render a ‘guilty’ verdict and are pricing in growing odds of default  FortuneFrance meets fiscal reality with a crunch  Financial TimesFrance’s budget offers no quick relief for bond markets  ING THINK Economic and financial analysis | ING THINKFrance’s Troubles Are Deepening as Investors Head for the Exit  Bloomberg.comFive French market hot spots on investors' radars  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Faced with the prospect of a far-right or a far-left president, the bond market doesn’t see France curbing its rapidly growing pile of debt anytime soon and has started weighing the possibility that the eurozone’s second largest economy could default.
That’s according to Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group. In a note Thursday, he said the cost of insurance against a French default is now the highest among the major EU countries and the U.K.
Early Friday, the signals sharpened further as France’s five-year sovereign credit default swap rose to 81 basis points. At the same time, its 10-year bond yields jumped to 4.989%, the highest since 2002, and the premium over equivalent German yields widened to 152 basis points, the most since the eurozone debt crisis in 2011.
Wizman warned: “The signal from France CDS pricing is that the OAT/Bund spread widening is due to higher sovereign default risk in France.”
Those metrics later came off their highs, but France’s fundamentals remain troubling, with anemic GDP growth, a budget deficit estimated at about 5.4% of GDP, and rising debt-service costs as yields jump.
Meanwhile, France’s debt-to-GDP ratio is expected to climb to 122% next year from 119% this year, and the government’s latest plan failed to halt the surge in bond yields as investors doubted its credibility.
“But our instinct is to also read the suddenly widening OAT/Bund yield spread as a ‘guilty’ verdict on the recent direction of France’s presidential politics,” Wizman wrote. “The problem in particular is political polarization, which has arisen—as it has across Europe—mainly over the immigration issue, rather than fiscal issues. But in France, neither the populist Left nor the populist Right are fiscal hawks.”
Indeed, far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is campaigning on a plan to have the central bank simply cancel its holdings of French debt.
And far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who is leading in the polls for the presidential race, has proposed tax cuts and vowed to bring down France’s retirement age to as low as 60, despite the already generous pension system eating up an ever bigger slice of the budget.
A runoff between the two candidates is expected next year, and Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) party is seen as the likely winner.
“As such, an outright default may be a low-probability event, but an RN-led presidency, with an adverse influence on the 2028 budget and credit-risk perceptions is a high-probability event, near 50%,” Wizman added.
He also pointed out that the presidential campaigns have barely begun, meaning the rhetoric around France’s debt, a potential default, and budgetary politics is set to heat up and further damage the perception of the government’s creditworthiness.
To be sure, France isn’t alone in facing high debt and market pressure on its bonds. The U.S. debt-to-GDP ratio is now 100%, and Japan’s is well above 200%.
But America’s GDP growth is much more robust, and Japan enjoys a large pool of built-in demand for its debt from domestic investors. By contrast France’s economy is projected to grow just 0.5% this year, and the government plans to issue over $380 billion in medium- and long-term debt next year.
Ales Koutny, head of international rates at Vanguard, told the Financial Times that demand for debt in markets that become the center of geopolitical issues “can disappear in times of crisis,” describing France as “long-term degrading credit.”
Similarly, Scope Ratings also flagged political risks when it cut France’s credit score to A+ from AA- last month, bringing it on par with Fitch and S&P Global Ratings.
In particular, the ratings firm cited the government’s difficulties in meeting self-imposed deficit targets, adding that the sharp rise in bond yields this year will further increase borrowing costs and make any debt solution even more painful.
“Scope expects political fragmentation to remain elevated beyond the 2027 presidential election, complicating the substantial fiscal consolidation required to stabilize public debt and increasing the risk that measures are diluted, delayed, or only partially implemented over coming years,” it warned. “This weakens Scope’s confidence in France’s ability to halt, let alone reverse, the deterioration of its public finances over the medium term.”

articles.title: ECB advances digital euro work and market framework updates in euro area - Traders Union
articles.summary: ECB advances digital euro work and market framework updates in euro area  Traders Union
articles.full_text:
The European Central Bank is expanding work beyond interest rate decisions as it updates its digital currency plans, market operations and governance across the euro area. The latest measures cover pilot outreach for the digital euro, legal changes to the Eurosystem monetary policy framework and responses on crypto regulation during August and September 2026.
Highlights
- ECB Governing Council launched two calls for expressions of interest in September 2026 for digital euro e-commerce pilots and private innovation partnerships, with application deadlines of 27 October and 9 November 2026.
- New amendments to Eurosystem monetary policy legal acts and guidelines to improve valuation processes will take effect from 30 November 2026.
- Nearly 10 million people, or 2.6% of the euro area population, responded to the ECB's euro banknote design survey, highlighting significant public interest in currency evolution.
Digital euro pilots and policy decisions
As reported by the European Central Bank, decisions published on 2 October set out progress on the digital euro and a series of operational and regulatory measures taken by its Governing Council during August and September 2026.
In external communications, the ECB says a 30 July press release detailed accessibility features for the digital euro app, with usability and accessibility testing due to start in 2027. On 15 September, the central bank also launched a call for expressions of interest for euro area e-commerce and mobile commerce merchants to join the digital euro pilot, with applications due by 27 October 2026.
On 28 September, the ECB issued a second call for expressions of interest aimed at private entities to examine how digital euro infrastructure could support innovation. Applications for that process are due by 9 November 2026.
In market operations, the Governing Council approves amendments to legal acts governing the Eurosystem monetary policy framework and adopts new guidelines intended to improve valuation processes within that framework. Those changes take effect from 30 November 2026.
Regulatory and governance impact across the euro area
The ECB also reports unusually strong public engagement in its survey on the future design of euro banknotes, with nearly 10 million respondents, equal to 2.6% of the euro area population. The turnout points to broad public interest in the future shape of euro cash as the institution develops both physical and digital forms of the currency.
On macroprudential policy, the Governing Council approves responses to the European Commission's consultation on the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, reflecting the growing complexity of oversight in the crypto sector. Other decisions include the appointment of Sigríður Dis Guðjónsdóttir as a non-voting member of the Market Infrastructure Board, alongside additional ECB opinions and governance extensions intended to strengthen supervisory and regulatory effectiveness.
Our earlier coverage of euro zone inflation and ECB rate-hike expectations explained how an upside inflation surprise—driven largely by higher energy prices and resilient activity—kept the case for further tightening alive. The article noted that markets were increasingly pricing a December deposit-rate increase as policymakers weighed the risk of energy costs feeding into broader price pressures.

articles.title: Eurozone Inflation Surges to 3.8%, Putting ECB Rate Path Back Under Pressure - Tekedia
articles.summary: Eurozone Inflation Surges to 3.8%, Putting ECB Rate Path Back Under Pressure  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
Eurozone inflation accelerated sharply in September, rising to 3.8% and reaching its highest level since September 2023, as a renewed energy shock pushed headline price growth well above market expectations and complicated the European Central Bank’s interest-rate outlook.
Annual inflation increased from 3.2% in August, exceeding the 3.6% consensus forecast and moving further away from the ECB’s 2% target. Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food components, was 2.5%, matching expectations.
The size of the headline increase is significant because it comes at a time when financial markets had begun to assume that the ECB could remain on hold as higher bond yields and tighter financial conditions did some of the central bank’s work.

September’s data challenges that assumption.
Energy prices were the dominant source of the acceleration, with energy inflation reaching 18.8%, its highest level since January 2023. The increase reflects the continuing impact of the Middle East conflict on oil and other energy costs, which are feeding through into household and business expenses across the region.
But the composition of the inflation increase is becoming more important for the ECB than the headline number alone. Core inflation remained elevated at 2.5%, suggesting that price pressures outside energy have not fully returned to levels consistent with the central bank’s target.
Harry Woolman, global capital markets analyst at Validus Risk Management, said the latest figures indicate that inflation may be broadening beyond the initial energy shock.
“While energy remains the main driver, September’s jump suggests it is now ‘more than an energy story’,” Woolman said, adding that the ECB’s October 29 meeting had become particularly important.
That has created a difficult policy environment for the ECB. Energy-driven inflation presents a familiar problem because monetary policy cannot directly increase oil supply or resolve geopolitical disruptions. Raising interest rates can, however, restrain demand and reduce the risk that a temporary energy shock becomes embedded in wages, services and broader price-setting behavior.
The danger for policymakers is the so-called second-round effect. If businesses pass higher energy and transportation costs to consumers, workers seek compensation for the resulting loss in purchasing power and companies then raise prices again to protect margins, an initial supply shock can become a more persistent inflation problem.
That is the experience policymakers remain particularly sensitive to after the inflation surge that followed the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Markets Reassess The ECB
The September inflation report arrives after investors had scaled back expectations for a sequence of ECB rate increases. ECB President Christine Lagarde had argued that higher bond yields were already tightening financial conditions, potentially reducing the need for the central bank to respond through additional policy-rate increases.
The latest inflation data makes that argument more difficult to sustain, according to Woolman.
“Markets had pared back expectations of consecutive rate rises in recent days, after President Lagarde suggested that higher bond yields were doing some of the tightening for the ECB. Today’s inflation reading makes that argument harder to sustain,” he said.
The contrast between market-driven tightening and central-bank action will now become more important. Higher government bond yields increase borrowing costs for households, companies and governments even when the ECB leaves its policy rate unchanged. In theory, that can restrain demand and help bring inflation down without another official rate increase.
But if inflation is accelerating rapidly enough, policymakers may still conclude that financial conditions are insufficiently restrictive, particularly if inflation expectations or wage demands begin to rise.
“A central bank mindful of the experience of 2022 will not want to wait for second-round effects to become entrenched before acting,” Woolman said.
The ECB therefore faces a trade-off between responding to an inflation shock that is being driven substantially by energy and avoiding excessive tightening that could weaken economic activity. According to analysts, that balance is becoming more difficult because the energy shock is occurring against a backdrop of geopolitical uncertainty rather than a purely temporary commodity-price movement. If energy prices remain elevated, the inflation impact could persist for longer than policymakers initially anticipated.
The 3.8% headline reading also complicates the communication challenge. Even if the ECB regards the underlying inflation trend as more important than the headline figure, households and financial markets respond to the prices they actually face. A sustained period of high energy inflation can influence inflation expectations even when core measures move more gradually.
The 2.5% core rate therefore matters. It is substantially closer to the ECB’s objective than the headline figure, but it remains above 2%. The September reading provides little evidence that the inflation problem has been fully resolved outside the energy shock.
The October 29 ECB meeting will consequently be closely watched for how policymakers distinguish between temporary supply-driven inflation and signs of broader price persistence.
For bond markets, the data is expected to bolster the upward pressure on yields if investors price in a higher probability of tighter monetary policy. For consumers and businesses, higher energy costs threaten to squeeze disposable income and profit margins. And for the ECB, the challenge is to prevent an external energy shock from turning into a domestic inflation cycle without unnecessarily damaging demand.
September’s inflation surge does not by itself determine the ECB’s next move. But it changes the policy backdrop materially. The central bank now has to assess not only how high inflation has risen, but how long the energy shock will last, and if underlying price pressures are easing fast enough, and higher market yields are providing sufficient restraint.
Those questions are likely to make the October meeting an important test of how the ECB responds when an inflation problem is driven initially by energy markets but begins to raise broader concerns about the persistence of price pressures.

articles.title: Ukraine Faces $27 Billion Defense Funding Gap as EU Rejects Early Loan Disbursement - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Ukraine Faces $27 Billion Defense Funding Gap as EU Rejects Early Loan Disbursement  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The Ukrainian government is scrambling to secure $27 billion in unfunded military and state expenditures through the end of 2026, prompting severe domestic austerity measures as international allies push back against requests for accelerated financial aid.
With the total cost of repelling the Russian invasion reaching an estimated $155 billion this year, Kyiv's budget is stretched to a breaking point. While the European Union has allocated substantial support, Brussels recently rejected a request to fast-track disbursements from a €90 billion ($98 billion) loan facility, demanding further progress on anti-corruption reforms and tax collection.
The widening shortfall threatens to disrupt the procurement of critical weaponry and the payment of military salaries just as Russian forces intensify their attacks on Ukraine's energy and telecommunications infrastructure ahead of a challenging winter.
The Anatomy of the $27 Billion Deficit
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi confirmed the staggering $27 billion gap during a late September address, outlining the stark realities of managing a wartime economy. The deficit represents a critical fraction of the $155 billion total war-related needs for the year, a figure that includes both domestic budget allocations and the value of in-kind military assistance such as Patriot interceptors and artillery provided by Western partners.
First Deputy Minister of Finance Roman Yermolychev provided a detailed breakdown of the shortfall during a recent economic forum in Kyiv. Approximately $7 billion is urgently needed to cover personnel pay and social benefits for service members. The remaining $20 billion is required for the procurement of weaponry, drones, missiles, and related logistical expenses.
To manage the immediate crisis, the government has adopted a strict priority order for state expenditures.
"This means strict austerity in public finances and postponing some nonessential spending," Koretskyi told reporters. "These funds are intended, among other things, to ensure payments to service members and support for their families. The remaining $20 billion is the subject of negotiations with our partners."
Domestic Austerity and Reallocation
The government plans to cover the $7 billion personnel shortfall through aggressive domestic fiscal measures. This includes freezing state-funded construction projects, suspending cultural programs, and delaying infrastructure initiatives linked to national resilience plans.
To boost state revenues for 2027, the Ukrainian parliament is deliberating a draft budget that includes a 1 percent increase in the Value Added Tax (VAT). However, these domestic efforts are insufficient to cover the $20 billion needed for physical military hardware, leaving Kyiv dependent on international capital.
Economist Oleksandra Myronenko of the Centre for Economic Strategy in Kyiv emphasized that in-kind military support has gradually decreased in relative terms, forcing the Ukrainian state to absorb a higher proportion of the financial burden directly. The shifting dynamic means that equipment previously donated from NATO stockpiles must now be purchased on the open market, sharply driving up the cash requirements for the Ministry of Defense.
The economic toll of the sustained conflict continues to erode Ukraine's domestic revenue base. Oleksandr Kravchenko, a senior government official, recently noted that the Ukrainian economy loses an estimated $45 million for every hour of nationwide air raid alerts, compounding the structural deficit caused by lower-than-expected tax revenues and soaring defense costs.
The European Union's Firm Stance
In an attempt to bridge the $20 billion hardware gap, Kyiv petitioned the European Union over the summer to accelerate the disbursement of a €90 billion loan package originally scheduled to be distributed through the end of 2027.
According to reports from Bloomberg, the EU disputed some of Ukraine's financial calculations and rejected the request for early payment. European officials argued that advancing the funds would merely create a more severe fiscal cliff in 2027. Instead, Brussels advised Kyiv to seek supplementary financing from other G7 partners, specifically identifying Canada, Japan, and the United States as potential alternative sources.
During a tense bilateral meeting at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reiterated that Brussels has €37 billion in budgetary support allocated for 2026. However, she emphasized that the release of these funds remains strictly conditional upon Ukraine's progress in implementing structural reforms.
The required reforms include decisive actions to combat the shadow economy, harmonize legislation with EU standards, and improve domestic tax collection—initiatives that have faced delays in the Ukrainian parliament.
Projecting the Long-Term Financial Burden
The current $27 billion gap is not an isolated crisis but a precursor to sustained structural deficits as the war transitions into a prolonged war of attrition. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has modeled Ukraine's financial trajectory, painting a sobering picture of the country's reliance on external financing over the next three years.
| Projected Ukrainian Funding Deficits (2026-2029) |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Year | Projected Deficit (USD) | Primary Drivers | 
|---|---|---|
| 2026 | $27 billion | Military salaries, air-defense procurement, infrastructure repair | 
| 2027 | $30 - $35 billion | Sustained military operations, exhausted domestic reserves | 
| 2028 | $17 billion | Post-conflict reconstruction, debt servicing | 
| 2029 | $2 billion | Long-term economic stabilization | 
| Source: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Estimates, September 2026 |  |  | 
The European Commission and Ukraine issued a joint statement confirming that while they have identified mechanisms to cover the 2026 budgetary needs, the actual release of the €45 billion tranche from the 2027 loan will not occur until the beginning of next year at the earliest.
Strategic Deadlines and Next Steps
As the winter approaches, the urgency of securing the unfunded $20 billion is paramount. Ukrainian officials have explicitly linked the availability of this funding to the military's operational capacity during the first quarter of 2027.
Without the necessary capital to procure interceptor missiles and frontline equipment, Ukraine's defense forces face an increased risk of logistical exhaustion. The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Defense are now conducting monthly coordination meetings with international donors to identify stopgap funding solutions.
Until a breakthrough is achieved in negotiations with the US, Japan, or the EU, Ukraine remains reliant on deep domestic cuts and the daily resilience of its heavily taxed civilian economy.

articles.title: US targets Iran auto, rail and metals sectors in new sanctions blitz - Iran International
articles.summary: US targets Iran auto, rail and metals sectors in new sanctions blitz  Iran International
articles.full_text:
The US Treasury sanctioned Iran’s automotive and rail sectors Thursday, expanding its campaign to some of the country’s largest industrial companies as Washington seeks to choke off Tehran’s sources of revenue with Operation Economic Outcast.
The Treasury said the sectors provide important sources of revenue and logistical capacity and are intertwined with IRGC patronage, trade-based money laundering and sanctions evasion.
“The Iranian regime's ability to fund its war machine and inflict terror on the world has been severely diminished thanks to Operation Economic Outcast,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
“Today’s action directly targets Iran’s enablers and lays the groundwork for the United States and our partners to drain the regime’s revenue once and for all.”
The automotive designations include Iran Khodro Company, SAIPA, Iran Khodro Diesel, Pars Khodro, Zamyad and Niroo Motor Shiraz.
Iran produced nearly 1.1 million vehicles in 2024, according to the International Organization of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers. Iran Khodro and SAIPA together account for more than 90% of the country’s domestic auto market.
The Treasury described the sector as a major remaining source of revenue for Iran and said Niroo Motor Shiraz had supplied more than 6,000 motorcycles for plainclothes intelligence agents working with the IRGC and Basij militia.
Foreign companies were also sanctioned for supporting Iran’s auto industry, including firms based in Indonesia, the UAE, Turkey and Hong Kong.
The Treasury said they supplied components to Iranian automakers or helped move parts into Iran, including shipments linked to Bahman Diesel, which it said produces vehicles for the Iranian armed forces and IRGC missile and drone units.
In the rail sector, the US government sanctioned the Islamic Republic of Iran Railway Company and Raja Passenger Trains Company, saying Tehran has increasingly relied on rail to move oil and sustain trade amid the US maritime blockade.
It also sanctioned Heavy Equipment Production Company (HEPCO) and its China-based subsidiary, saying HEPCO machinery has been used by the IRGC and Quds Force to build underground facilities and military training sites.
The metals sanctions targeted companies in the UAE and Germany over dealings with Iranian steel producers.
The Treasury also designated Ramin Keshvardoust and Mehnoosh Poursaraf Hamedani and companies tied to their steel and financial network in Iran, China and elsewhere.
The US government accused the network of facilitating tens of millions of dollars in Iranian steel and oil shipments and laundering transactions through Iran’s shadow banking system.
In a separate action Thursday, the Treasury targeted the Russia-linked A7 Network, describing it as a “shadow banking network” used by Iran to evade sanctions.
It said A7’s sub-agents formed a money-laundering and sanctions-evasion mechanism linked to Russian illicit finance that Iran used to move funds, including for oil sales and weapons procurement.
Operation Economic Outcast was launched in August to cut off Iran’s remaining sources of revenue and expand sanctions pressure beyond oil into industrial sectors that Tehran still relies on for trade, logistics and foreign currency.
The Treasury says the campaign is designed to isolate companies and financial channels that help Iran move funds, sustain industrial production and circumvent US restrictions.

articles.title: Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU - theguardian.com
articles.summary: Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU  theguardian.com
articles.full_text:
Andy Burnham has opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way”, as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.
The prime minister used a series of interviews after his emotional Labour conference speech to spell out how wide-ranging his consideration of Britain’s future with Brussels could be because Brexit had caused “more harm than good”.
Burnham said the government could keep the current arrangements, seek a customs union, return to the single market or “go all the way” in what would be full EU membership. Speaking to the BBC, he said ministers would examine “what is doable” and the “pros and cons” of each option.
Asked whether he wanted the UK to rejoin the bloc, the prime minister told Radio 4’s Today programme he wanted to “look at the options”. He added: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.”
It is a significant shift from the position Labour fought the 2024 election on. Its manifesto explicitly ruled out returning to the EU single market or customs union, as well as restoring freedom of movement.
A customs union would bring Britain much closer to the EU on trade in goods. The UK and EU would apply the same tariffs to imports from elsewhere, removing trade barriers businesses have faced after Brexit. But it would not on its own put Britain back inside the wider single market or remove every border check.
If Britain were to rejoin the single market, it would be a significant step with the country having to accept closer alignment with EU rules.
“There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each,” Burnham told the BBC.
Although Burnham has not set out any timetables or specifics, to “go all the way” would mean considering EU membership. He went further in his interviews on Wednesday than his conference speech in which he told delegates Britain could not keep avoiding a decision about its long-term relationship with its largest trading partner.
The prime minister has vowed to set out different choices facing the country around the time of the UK-EU summit in November. “We’ve been in a rut. The country hasn’t been working for people as it should,” he told BBC Breakfast. The summit was originally supposed to take place in July under Keir Starmer but was postponed after his resignation.
While Britain will take part in the Erasmus + scheme again in 2027, the EU has authorised talks at the summit on closer electricity-market links, with negotiations on food trade and youth mobility still under way.
Burnham argued in his conference speech that leaving the EU had weakened Britain’s cooperation with EU countries on migration and said the summit would assess how the two parties could work more closely. “We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of the century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” Burnham said in his speech on Tuesday in Liverpool.
“I cannot say to you that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners. And there are different options.”
The prime minister was more cautious when pressed on help households could receive in the budget given the looming winter and rising energy and fuel costs. Burnham said he was considering “everything that might help people” including whether to scrap planned fuel duty increases.
“The question I’ve got is: ‘How many can I afford?’” he told BBC Breakfast. The chancellor, John Healey, has said “fiscal discipline” will be at the heart of his budget despite facing calls to offer people more help with the cost of living.

articles.title: Trump ramps up pressure on US Republicans to end US clock switching - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Trump ramps up pressure on US Republicans to end US clock switching  Al JazeeraTrump appears to share personal phone number of US senator in ploy to push permanent daylight savings  The GuardianTrump, Cotton tussle over daylight savings after cell phone number leak  The HillTrump shares Republican senator's phone number in feud over time switch  ReutersTrump reveals Tom Cotton’s phone number in daylight saving time standoff  washingtonpost.com
articles.full_text:
United States President Donald Trump has increased the pressure on US Senate Republicans to make Daylight Saving Time permanent, singling out one of the body’s members for stalling legislation to end the twice-a-year changing of clocks.
In a social media post on Saturday, Trump blasted US Senator Tom Cotton for “holding up” the Sunshine Protection Act, which Trump has personally opted to call the “No More Changing of Clocks Act”.
“For some reason, Tom is stopping the Bill and, in the Senate, it’s very easy to do, it only takes one!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social account about the Arkansas Republican. “It should pass overwhelmingly, in a Bipartisan fashion”.
“Nobody wants to spend their precious time running all over the place, turning Clocks back twice a year and, having sunshine in the afternoon is better than early in the morning!” he added.
Trump went even further, publishing what he claimed was Cotton’s phone number as he implored Arkansas residents to pressure him. The move echoed a moment during the 2016 Republican presidential primaries, when then-candidate Trump gave out US Senator Lindsey Graham’s number after the former rival criticised him.
Al Jazeera called the number listed in Trump’s post, but an automated message stated the voicemail box was full. Cotton’s spokesperson and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.
The president has routinely pushed Senate Republicans to pass legislation mandating year-round daylight saving, which would end Americans’ decades-long practice of changing their clocks twice a year to increase daylight hours. On Friday, Trump urged the US Senate to approve the bill, which passed the US House in July by a 308-117 vote.
Cotton has previously opposed the bill, arguing in a US Senate floor speech last year that farmers, construction workers, commuters and children heading to school would begin their days in the dark during the winter.
Trump disputed that argument in a separate post on Saturday, saying the bill “would be a very nice and easy WIN for the Republican Party”.
“If Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give them an extra hour of daylight and, more importantly, they wouldn’t have to run all over their houses, farms, workplaces, and everywhere else, twice a year, having to change their Clocks, and often forgetting to do so”, Trump wrote.
Trump, an avid golfer, also highlighted what he considered to be another selling point of the bill: the North American Professional Golfers’ Association (PGA) tour.
“The PGA TOUR, as an example, needs more Daylight in the afternoon in order to finish their Tournaments”, he wrote in a post, which included a letter from PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp supporting the bill. “Likewise, regular Golfers, Tennis Players, Hunters and, perhaps more importantly, Farmers who want more Daylight to play or work.”
The US president, who spent part of Saturday at his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, indicated in a subsequent post that he had received personal feedback on the proposal: “I don’t know about anyone else, but a table full of very distinguished people just told me that they HATE, immediately after a mandatory time change, going home at night – and it’s DARK. It’s depressing!”
In 1974, the US Congress briefly adopted year-round daylight saving time in response to the country’s energy crisis. But Congress repealed the law less than a year later over safety concerns as children commuted to school before sunrise.
US senators left Washington this week and have no set plans to return until after the November 3 midterm elections.
Some members, such as Senator John Kennedy, weren’t optimistic that Senate Republican Leader John Thune would bring the bill up for a vote before polling day.
“It’s dead as disco,” the Louisiana Republican told Reuters this week of Trump’s push to make daylight saving time permanent. “My sense is it would have trouble passing … I don’t think the leader is going to bring it up.”

articles.title: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes - The Kyiv Independent
articles.summary: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes  The Kyiv IndependentUkraine war briefing: Kyiv to increase oil refinery attacks because of Moscow’s winter strategy, Zelenskyy says  The GuardianEXCLUSIVE: Ukraine will hit Russian refineries in response to Moscow's 'new doctrine' of airstrikes, Zelenskiy says  ReutersPutin has told military leaders to abandon rules of war, Zelenskyy says  Financ...
articles.full_text:
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties, said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities.
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran. While Zelensky has expressed his willingness to try an energy ceasefire, the American president's pleas appear to have gained little traction in Moscow.
In order to help double down on striking Russian energy sites, Ukraine will continue to produce its own long-range ballistic missiles. On Oct. 1, Zelensky announced Ukraine's domestically developed FP-7 ballistic missile was used in combat against Russia for the first time.
Zelensky told Reuters he has already called on the missile's manufacturer, Fire Point, to prepare longer-range missiles.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9? We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be [ready] this autumn, I'm sure," Zelensky said.
On Oct. 3, Zelensky said Ukraine had responded to Russian strikes on civilian targets by using long-range missiles to hit a facility in Russia's Samara region as well as an "Iskander" missile systems in the Bryansk region.

We sit down with David McAllister, the chair of the European Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee. He talks to us about the security threats facing Europe, and what defence gaps the EU urgently needs to close. For McAllister, the EU is "not at war with the Russian Federation, but we are no longer at peace with Russia". He also believes that the EU is not, as yet, capable of making sovereign decisions in certain areas of defence "because we are too dependent on US capabilities."
Asked about the worsening security situation that Europe faces, McAllister says: "We need to establish a fully fledged European defence by the end of this decade. We need to be able to defend ourselves against all the imminent threats we are facing. And that means spending more, but also spending more effectively, because it is taxpayers' money that we are spending in large numbers. There are certain military capabilities that we don't have in Europe, for the time being. There are fields in which we have to move ahead. I'm talking about ammunition and anti-drone systems. I'm talking about satellite intelligence. I'm talking about air-to-air refuelling. I'm talking about air defence in general. These are fields where we are not in a situation to take sovereign decisions because we are too dependent on US capabilities. We have to close these gaps urgently."
Speaking of threats, McAllister asserts that "we are not at war with the Russian Federation, but we are longer at peace with Russia. We have every day, every week, violations of our airspace, attacks on our critical infrastructure, cyberattacks. That is also why it was so positive that the Federal Republic of Germany got the immediate solidarity of all 26 other member states (after the drone attack on Leipzig airport, attributed to Russian special services). An attack on one of us is an attack on all of us. And that's why it's correct to sanction the Russian Federation, to further sanction individuals, but also to come up with new additional ideas for how we can better protect our critical infrastructure."
We ask about German Chancellor Friedrich Merz leading the charge to secure hundreds of billions of euros in cuts from the proposed EU budget, also known as the Multiannual Financial Framework, or MFF. Would Merz's proposal not hurt cohesion, regional development and social spending that EU member states actually benefit from?
"We are now entering crunch time, and we still have a lot of work ahead of us," McAllister concedes. "There will be controversial debates, but I'm very sure that in the end, as always, there will be a last-minute solution. If you look back over the last 10, 15, 20 years, there have always been heated discussions about the size and the dimension of the MFF and who will pay how much and for what. [EU Council President] Antonio Costa has been clear. He wants an agreement on the next MFF, starting on the 1st of January in 2028. I would welcome that because we need the year 2027 for the necessary legislative work and so that everyone who receives EU money has clarity and can plan better for the years 2028 to 2034."
In Germany, the far-right AfD party surged in recent regional elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania. What are the implications for conservatives, for Christian Democrats and for the European People's Party?
"We have different political conditions in the 27 member states, and we have different strategies," McAllister says. "I can only say, as a German Christian Democrat, our strategy towards the AfD is that if we are convinced of something and we propose legislation, and by chance the AfD supports it, then we accept this. But they are our policies. We never support proposals coming from the AfD. We never actively engage with the AfD. We are strictly against this. Why? Because the AfD is questioning the fundamentals of the Federal Republic of Germany and also of the European Union. They are against the EU. They are against the euro. They are against NATO. They are pro-Putin and they are following a right-wing populist radical course. And that is not where the EPP should be. We are the party of common sense and that is in the centre."

articles.summary: Europe to reach 80% decarbonised power but miss its renewables target by 2030  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Europe's power sector is set to surpass 80% decarbonised generation by 2030, but will miss its flagship renewables target by the same date, according to Wood Mackenzie's Europe Power Markets Strategic Planning Outlook 2026, which covers 35 national markets through 2060. Total power demand would rise 66% by 2050, driven first by data centres and then by the electrification of end uses.
Power demand reshapes investment priorities
Total power demand would reach 4,103 TWh by 2030, 11% above 2025 levels, before climbing to 6,152 TWh by 2050, a 66% increase from current levels, according to the research firm. Near term, data centres are the primary driver of this growth, before falling electricity prices shift the economics of electrification from the 2030s onward. Strengthening grid infrastructure, as illustrated by the financing mobilised through La BEI et BNP Paribas mobilisent 700 millions d'euros pour les réseaux électriques or the UK's programme to speed up electricity connections, will determine the system's ability to absorb this demand. The consolidation of power sector players, illustrated by TotalEnergies' creation of Integrated Power Germany to consolidate its electricity operations, also reflects this market dynamic.
Electric vehicle adoption would accelerate, underpinned by bans on new sales of internal combustion vehicles, with consumption growing from 39 TWh in 2025 to 577 TWh by 2050, a 15-fold increase. On-grid hydrogen would scale from near zero to 417 TWh over the same period. Heat pump demand would expand more than fivefold by 2060, though high upfront costs and unfavourable electricity-to-gas price ratios would keep most markets short of their national targets.
Company TotalEnergies: company profile TTE.PA
Northern and Southern Europe move at different paces
Northern Europe would record the strongest absolute demand growth, at 81% by 2050, versus 52% for Southern Europe, according to Wood Mackenzie. Overall demand would sit around 2% lower than the firm's previous forecast, as heat and hydrogen electrification progress more slowly than anticipated. Risks run both ways, however: geopolitical uncertainty and commodity price pressure could slow consumption growth, while prolonged fossil fuel disruption could instead accelerate it and trigger additional decarbonisation policies.
On the supply side, solar photovoltaic capacity is expected to nearly double to 637 GWac by 2030, adding around 61 GW per year. Onshore wind would add 17 GW per year to reach 346 GW, while offshore wind would reach 73 GW by 2030 before accelerating to 148 GW by 2035, a timeline delayed by supply chain pressures and investor uncertainty. Renewables would account for 65% of supply across the 35 markets studied by 2030, then 83% by 2050.
Missed renewables target, gas extends its presence
On an EU27 basis, the renewables share would reach 63.7% by 2030, below both the Fit-for-55 target of 65% and the REPowerEU goal of 69%, according to the report. Battery storage would more than triple, from 47 GW to 163 GW by 2030, one of the largest near-term capital deployment opportunities in the European power sector. Germany, the UK, Italy and Poland would account for over half of that growth.
Natural gas generation would average 6% higher between 2026 and 2040 than in Wood Mackenzie's previous forecast, as offshore wind downgrades created a supply gap filled by gas. Gas capacity would rise 5% to 273 GW by 2030, even as fleet utilisation falls from 27% to 22%. Coal generation would halve, from 457 TWh in 2025 to 237 TWh by 2030, before the EU27 fleet exits the mix entirely by 2050, while power supply from gas would decline 45% by 2060.
Wood Mackenzie's message to investors
Mohammed Alraood, Research Analyst Europe Power at Wood Mackenzie, said Europe's power transition "is on track, but it is not evenly distributed." He added that "rising emissions costs will force structural decisions that markets are only beginning to price in" and that "gas remains in the mix, not for volume but for the moments renewables cannot deliver."
According to Wood Mackenzie, the pace of the transition will depend on grid investment and interconnector expansion, two variables that no forecast can fully determine. The firm expects the region's commitment to the energy transition to be sustained, while noting that investment opportunities in new capacity will not be uniform across markets.

Vladimir Putin’s regime has been accused of covering up an outbreak of the ‘plague’ in Russia which has killed one person and forced another 189 into quarantine.
Reports claim the country’s chief infectious diseases doctor Anna Popova has travelled to Irkutsk in Siberia to take charge of the situation, with public events cancelled across the region.
Officials also ordered residents of neighbouring Baikalsk to avoid travelling to Shelekhov, where the outbreak is reported to have taken place, although the message was later deleted.
There are also claims that antibiotics in the region have sold out.
The outbreak is linked to the death of a laboratory assistant,Daria Shipilova, at Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute.
Some reports claim the 28-year-old fell ill while on an expedition on the border between Russia and Mongolia, while others say she was infected at the Institute after ‘breaking a test tube’.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
She is said to have died at Shelekhov District Hospital, which is now under quarantine, along with the Institute, with a total on 189 people under lockdown
Governor Igor Kobzev said mass events had been cancelled following a ‘particularly dangerous infectious disease’.
Russian news outlet Mash said: ‘Doctors and Rospotrebnadzor [Russia’s public health watchdog] are investigating the circumstances of the infection and carrying out anti-epidemic measures.’
News of the outbreak was posted in Telegram channel Nezygar, which compared the authorities’ reaction to those of China when Covid broke out.
‘The situation in Shelekhov, Irkutsk region, where a plague quarantine has been declared, resembles the Wuhan case,” it said.
‘An employee of the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, Shipilova, broke a test tube containing pathogens while at work, after which she left the laboratory and travelled home to Shelekhov.’
Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov, who now lives in America, criticised authorities for their response and for allowing ‘a lot of nonsense’ to circulate.
‘Someone working at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk wears a protective anti-plague suit,’ he said. ‘If you break a test tube, the likelihood of infection is actually very low.
‘The story about the test tube? It’s laughable.
‘It’s not as if the plague just flies out of the test tube, after all.
‘That’s not how it works. In short, it doesn’t matter to the general public. They’ll believe the “dropped test tube” story.’
Popova’s presence in Irkutsk meant it is a ‘terrible, critical situation’, he said, adding that a cover-up was underway and ‘we will not be told what really happened’.

Ethiopian federal forces have entered the capital of the northern Tigray region and seized its airport, witnesses said Saturday, reversing a takeover by rebels from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. The TPLF has been fighting against pro-government forces since September 23, raising fears of an all-out civil war similar to that of 2020-2022.
Ethiopian federal forces entered the Tigray state capital on Saturday, a humanitarian source told AFP, after residents reported that the region's rebels had abandoned the city.
Fighting erupted on September 23 in northern Ethiopia as the rebel Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched attacks into neighbouring states, raising fears of a return to the devastating 2020-2022 civil war.
But federal forces and pro-government militias have pushed them back in recent days and were heading north towards the regional capital, Mekelle.

"Ethiopian federal forces and allied forces have reportedly been observed in Mekelle city... across various locations," a humanitarian source said told AFP late Saturday, citing reports from staff on the ground.
Earlier, a journalist in the city told AFP that "TPLF militants and leaders are leaving Mekelle".
He said government offices and police stations had been left without security personnel.
The journalist could not be reached for more details, as telecommunications networks have been severely disrupted in Tigray since hostilities, making the few bits of information that emerge difficult to verify.
Regional summit
"I am concerned that government and public property could be exposed to looting because there are no security forces in the city," a local resident told AFP.
"Lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order," added another resident.
Neither the spokesperson for the Ethiopian National Defense Forces nor that of federal Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has responded to AFP's requests for comment.
