A diplomatic source told AFP that a mini-summit on Sunday would bring together the presidents of Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, as well as the head of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), Abdel Fattah al-Burhane, in Alamein, Egypt, on the sidelines of an African Business Forum.
The TPLF has long been the dominant force in Tigray, ousting a government-appointed administration earlier this year.
In a video message on Thursday, its leader Debretsion Gebremichael implied the TPLF would continue guerrilla-style attacks as they did when Mekelle fell to government forces in 2020.
Their insurgent campaign ultimately led to the TPLF retaking the city in mid-2021.
"We operate under a strategy to strike the enemy wherever we choose," Debretsion said.
Neighbourhood tensions
The conflict has triggered a breakdown in Ethiopia's relations with Eritrea and Egypt, which Ethiopia accuses of supporting the rebels.
Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara on Thursday, while Eritrea responded that it would "sever all diplomatic ties".

Eritrea accuses landlocked Ethiopia of planning to invade and seize access to its coastline.
The TPLF's Debretsion said in his video message that "the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea".
Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat without explanation, prompting a reciprocal move by Cairo.
Counter-offensive
The rebels initially made advances in neighbouring Afar and Amhara states, working alongside local militias.
But they were pushed back this week, and the government launched a counter-offensive into Tigrayan territory along three axes towards Mekelle, according to the Critical Threats Project, part of the American Enterprise Institute think tank.
There were reports that Mekelle's airport, on the southern approach to the city, had fallen to a pro-government militia on Friday.
But social media accounts are difficult to verify, media access is heavily restricted and there have been significant communications blackouts.
Earlier, a humanitarian source told AFP on condition of anonymity that the TPLF had been entirely pushed out of Afar.
The TPLF ruled all of Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018, when it was marginalised with the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, who hails from the Oromia region.
The tensions led to a civil war from 2020 to 2022 – one of the deadliest in the world in recent times – that left more than 600,000 dead, according to the African Union.
The Pretoria peace agreement of 2022, brokered by African institutions and Washington, maintained an uneasy calm until last year, but was never fully implemented.

articles.title: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes - The Guardian
articles.summary: Bangkok at breaking point as floods turn streets into stagnant lakes  The GuardianThai PM Anutin orders urgent nationwide water drainage ahead of new downpours  The Straits TimesThai Airways suspends chief executive as carrier reviews flood crisis response  FlightGlobalFlooding persists in 26 provinces and Bangkok  Bangkok PostAt least 23 dead in Thailand floods, Bangkok airport in chaos  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Bangkok is used to absorbing the sudden afternoon downpours that inundate the city during the rainy season. Even streets in many central high-rise districts can briefly turn into rivers, with rats and cockroaches racing out of sewers and taking temporary refuge on trees and buildings as the subterranean world is flushed out.
But every city has a breaking point, and this year rain fell so fast and so hard that whole neighbourhoods of the Thai capital have been transformed, not into rivers, but stagnant lakes. In parts of the city, roughly 300mm of rain – the equivalent of half a year of average rainfall in London – fell in about two days.
About 40 people died in flood-related incidents, according to the government. A number of the deaths were from drowning and several from accidental electrocution. Thousands of people stayed in more than 230 shelters across the city, authorities said.
Suleemas Kurangkul, a 73-year-old resident of a block of flats whose ground floor stairs are still under water, said last weekend’s rain was not the usual evening storm but was constant, “like all day, all night”.
“The water just kept rising,” said Suleemas, whose flat is above the waterline on the second floor. By the time she and her neighbours received a mobile phone warning, it was too late, and the street-level water was waist-high.
The 1970s Khlong Chan flat compound in north-east Bangkok where Suleemas lives has become a symbol of the disaster. Photos have been shared across Thailand of the flats rising out of the brownish water, with the rooftops of parked cars barely peeking above the surface, although the authorities had managed to drain away the worst of it by Thursday.
Later in the week, during a brief respite in the rain, Suleemas said the water had receded somewhat. “People are so happy to see the sunshine,” she said. “Yet, the smell is getting stronger. So much debris and rubbish floating all over the place.”
Built on a vast floodplain of the Chao Phraya River, Bangkok, a megacity of millions, relies on a network of muddy canals to drain water, as well as pumps and dikes. But concrete construction has destroyed much of the canal network, and the city is unable to cope.
The government has declared a flood disaster across all 50 of the city’s districts. Some neighbourhoods have turned into dystopian scenes, with people using blow-up paddling pools or, in one case, a floating fridge, as boats to reach their homes. One man was arrested for riding a jetski along a main road.
“It’s a lesson,” said Chaleerat Chamrasporn, 55, a resident. “The kids are into doomsday-themed content, so now they can see what the ‘end of the world’ is actually like, or rather, that this is just the beginning.”
Flooding has also disrupted Bangkok’s main Suvarnabhumi airport, with about half of Thai Airways’ workforce unable to report for work at one point this week, causing thousands of items of luggage to pile up and forcing flight cancellations. Many schools have closed, and with much of the capital in gridlock even people in less affected areas have been stuck at home.
Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, told reporters that Bangkok’s metropolitan area was still at risk from flood waters flowing in from the north, and said a war room had been set up to monitor the situation. Thailand’s weather agency has forecast more heavy rain for next week.
It is part of a pattern that seems to be setting in this part of the world. South-east Asia has already seen a worsening of extreme floods, scientists say, a trend that is set to worsen as fossil fuel pollutants bake the planet further. Hot seas evaporate more water and warm air can hold more moisture, allowing downpours to crash down with far more force.
“In central Thailand, I can see from my maps, we have already seen a small but significant trend towards extreme rainfall,” said Nikolaos Skliris, an ocean scientist at the University of Southampton who has studied heavy rain in the region. “In the long-term, all models show this will be amplified – more rainfall, and more extreme rainfall.”
It is too early for scientists to attribute these particular rains to climate breakdown without doing a study. They were caused by a low-pressure system that moved from an unusually warm South China Sea over Cambodia and Vietnam before getting stuck above Bangkok, which was fairly cool, data from Copernicus Climate Pulse showed.
The picture is complicated by the emergence of an abnormally strong El Niño, a cyclical weather pattern that brings record heat and more violent extremes around the world. Its presence typically leads to drier summer conditions in south-east Asia but recent research suggests it still exacerbates days with extreme rainfall.
Naim Laeni, a consultant and part-time university lecturer who co-authored a study on Bangkok’s flood resilience, said authorities had underestimated the strength of the rains, which persisted for days. The city’s drainage canals can handle about 60mm of rain an hour, rising to 80mm in upgraded sections, but localised bursts exceeded this while leaving too little time between periods of stress.
“The government did not communicate the seriousness,” said Laeni. “Usually in Bangkok we receive heavy rain for a few hours, not for days.”
Neighbouring Myanmar has suffered from the same weather system, with flash floods and blocked roads complicating rescue efforts in the country.
Rescuers were pulling bodies from a landslide that devastated the village of Ka Det Nge Htein in Myanmar’s south at the weekend. That disaster had already claimed nine lives, and eight more people are missing under the mud in another village, local officials said.
Civil war across the country, and a junta that restricts the media, have made it hard to get information, and hampered aid organisations.
Back in Bangkok, pumping stations have been operating at full capacity, but it could be days before the waters fully drain.
At her apartment complex, Suleemas said she would stay where she was with her neighbours.
“It’s hard, yes, very hard,” she said. “But together we are fighting and biting through it. When we get together to help one another like this, our spirit can keep us on our feet; we can get through it all together.”
Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

articles.title: Soaring Energy Prices Keep Pushing European Inflation. It Just Now Reached a Three-Year High. - inkl
articles.summary: Soaring Energy Prices Keep Pushing European Inflation. It Just Now Reached a Three-Year High.  inkl
articles.full_text:
Eurozone inflation kept climbing in September, fueled by soaring energy prices. The rate clocked in at 3.8% last month, a three-year high and above expectations. The figure is also up 0.6 percentage points from August, and core inflation stood at 2.5%, in line with expectations.
Energy led the increase, standing at 18.8%, compared with 14.3% in August. It was followed by "followed by services (3.2%, compared with 3.0% in August), food, alcohol & tobacco (1.4%, compared with 1.1% in August) and non-energy industrial goods (1.1%, compared with 1.2% in August)," Eurostat noted.
Earlier this month, the ECB raised interest rates, noting that the war between the U.S. and Iran keeps putting pressure on prices.
The benchmark rate now stands at 2.5% compared to the previous 2.25%. The body noted in a statement that the decision "underscores the Governing Council's commitment to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term."
The body went on to say that its baseline projections now stand at 3% this year, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028. Core inflation, in turn, is set to be stickier: "the baseline foresees 2.5% in 2026, 2.6% in 2027 and 2.3% in 2028. Compared with June, the baseline projection for inflation in 2026 is unchanged, while it has been revised up for 2027 and 2028," the document says.
The ECB warned that outlooks remain "highly uncertain, with risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for economic growth."
"In relation to the energy shock, the updated scenarios put together by staff illustrate the broad range of outcomes for how growth and inflation would evolve under different assumptions about its intensity and duration, as well as its indirect and second-round effects," the document adds.
Staffers concluded that the decision leaves the Governing Council "well positioned to navigate the uncertainty caused by the conflict." However, it added that it "stands ready to adjust all of its instruments within its mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission."

articles.title: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, will it curb prices?  Al JazeeraG7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat  BBCUS backs down from fuel export ban threat as G7 agrees to release 100mn barrels  Financial TimesG7 Leaders’ Statement on global energy security and market stability  GOV.UKWorld in Brief: G7 to release oil reserves; Russia targets Kyiv’s bridges  The Economist
articles.full_text:
The Group of Seven (G7) countries have agreed to release 100 billion barrels of crude oil and diesel from emergency reserves over several months in an effort to reduce soaring energy prices after pressure from United States President Donald Trump.
The US and Israel’s war on Iran, as well as Russia’s war on Ukraine, have triggered a spike in global oil and diesel prices.
“The emergency release by G7 members will put some downward pressure on prices, particularly global diesel prices. However, the impact would be short-lived given that this is just a temporary solution to the supply crunch,” Hamad Hussain, a climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, told Al Jazeera.
Oil prices jumped on Thursday and settled up more than $4 a barrel. Global diesel prices also hit a record high last Friday with the average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) of diesel at $6.50, up from $5.61 a month earlier, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).
In a statement on Thursday, the G7, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the US, with the European Union also represented, said there will also be a “substantial diesel release within the first 20 days” and discussions over “additional diesel releases as necessary” will be held in the coming days.
Will the G7’s energy release stabilise the global energy market?
Here’s what we know:
What has the G7 announced?
After a video conference of G7 leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday, the group said in a joint statement: “Taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled, we will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels.”
Earlier this week, the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Executive Director Fatih Birol said that members had released about two-thirds of the 400-million-barrel agreement.
The G7 energy release will begin immediately and last for four months and will include a substantial diesel release for 20 days. It is not clear how many oil and diesel stocks each member of the group will release.
“We will convene in the context of the IEA in the coming days to discuss the possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary,” the statement said.
“We will coordinate maintenance schedules across G7 refineries to prevent simultaneous capacity shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible,” it added.
The G7 also urged member countries to refrain from imposing export restrictions on energy products among themselves.
Earlier this week, the Trump administration had threatened to impose a ban on US diesel exports and also pressured Europe to release its emergency diesel stocks to help ease soaring diesel prices.
Why are oil and diesel prices so high?
Global energy prices have been soaring due to the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which has disrupted energy exports from the Gulf. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy installations have also disrupted global energy supplies.
The former head of the International Energy Agency’s Oil Industry and Markets Division, Neil Atkinson, told Al Jazeera that there are three key factors contributing to the decline in global diesel supply.
First, “there isn’t diesel coming out of the Middle East to Europe, and Europe took quite a lot of diesel from Saudi Arabia and from Kuwait”.
Second, “Russia has now ceased to export diesel at all” due to “the attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries”.
“And China is no longer exporting diesel,” he added.
“We’re in a situation where demand remains relatively high and is likely to stay high because of the agricultural harvesting season.”
According to data from the Joint Organizations Data Initiative (JODI) and the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), the US is the world’s largest producer and exporter of diesel. It produces about 240.5 million tonnes and exports around 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day.
Russia is the world’s second-largest diesel exporter, supplying 783,400 barrels per day (bpd) to the global market. Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest producer of diesel at 58.4 million tonnes, but it consumes a large portion of its diesel domestically.
Will the G7 energy release bring prices down?
After the G7 announcement, French President Macron, who had co-chaired the meeting, said the group’s move to release the oil will “bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.
The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly dropped below $100 a barrel after the G7 announcement, but rose to about $102 in the evening.
Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets, told Al Jazeera that the G7 energy release was “very much needed”, but the group’s announcement was just to ease off pressure on the energy market.
“The actual structure changes about who is going to release [the energy stocks] and what and where the bans will be lifted, remains an important component in terms of the market,” he said.
Aslam added that by Sunday night, especially before the markets open, the added pressure on energy prices will come off. “But going into Monday morning … we could potentially see the reversal in the market,” he added.
Atkinson, the energy expert, said the G7’s fuel release is welcome but “doesn’t deal with the fundamental problem that the global supply remains lower than normal”.
Atkinson told Al Jazeera that “seven months after this war started in the Middle East, we are still in a situation where the global supply of crude oil or products remains significantly below pre-war levels”.
“We are now in a situation where the focus is on end use of products, mainly diesel, which is what we’re talking about here,” he added.
What has Trump said?
Soaring diesel prices have been a source of tension for the Trump administration and Republicans who fear this will cost them votes in the upcoming November midterm elections.
Last week, Trump pressured Ukraine to stop attacking Russian diesel facilities amid the war.
Then, on Thursday this week, the US president told reporters that his administration “may” ask European countries to release diesel stocks, shortly after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Europe to “immediately” tap its reserves.
Trump also threatened to ban US diesel exports if Europe did not release emergency diesel stocks.
But on Friday, Trump told reporters at the White House that Washington would not impose a diesel export ban. He said the plan was never really on the table.
“Europe has a lot of diesel, and they’re going to be making a major world contribution, and so are we. And we’re not going to be doing the export ban. We’re going to be doing what we’re supposed to do,” Trump said.
“Trump is scared by diesel prices above $6, which is a price jump of 70 percent compared to before he started the war. This is likely to get worse with US diesel inventories at their lowest seasonal level since records began in 1982.
“So if there is not enough diesel being produced because of the US-Israeli war on Iran, and diesel reserves have been used up, the only way to bring more diesel to the US market is by exporting less,” Frederic Schneider, a nonresident senior fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, told Al Jazeera on Friday.
After the G7 announcement, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately.”
The White House is also reportedly preparing an executive order to tackle record-high US diesel prices that could be unveiled as early as next week, two people familiar with the process told the Reuters news agency.
Schneider noted that countries are also concerned about high energy prices since diesel and gasoline are important for economies and fulfil different roles.
“While gasoline fuels cars, diesel fuels anything from trucks, freight trains, ships, tractors, harvesters, construction machinery, mining equipment and backup generators. This means gasoline is used more by consumers while diesel is mostly used by producers, meaning a diesel price shock spreads into the price of almost everything else, most prominently food, building materials and anything delivered by truck,” he added.
Farmers are hit twice because diesel prices are rising at the same time as fertiliser prices, both of which have been pushed up by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
“A higher diesel price therefore acts like a tax on production and logistics, while higher gasoline prices act like a tax on consumers directly. Like higher gasoline prices, higher diesel prices risk stagflation by pushing up inflation while simultaneously squeezing margins in transport and agriculture, meaning central banks find [themselves] in a dilemma between cutting rates [helping producers] and raising rates [cutting inflation],” he said.

articles.title: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’ - The Guardian
articles.summary: OpenAI safety leader quits, warning AI company’s culture is ‘broken’  The GuardianI Quit OpenAI Because Its Culture Is Broken  The AtlanticOpenAI fires workers for 'mishandling sensitive information'  BBCOpenAI safety employee quits, says 'time for trial and error is over'  ReutersAI needs safety layers like nuclear plants: ex-OpenAI engineer  Yahoo Finance UK
articles.full_text:
A safety leader at OpenAI has quit the company, warning that its culture was broken and that AI firms were not “being nearly careful enough” about developing the technology.
David Robinson, who led the writing of safety reports that accompanied the ChatGPT developer’s product releases, explained his resignation in an essay headlined, “I quit OpenAI because its culture is broken”.
Robinson wrote that a cultural overhaul was needed at cutting-edge AI firms and incidents such as a “swarm” of OpenAI agents – AI programmes operating autonomously without human oversight – attacking the AI startup Hugging Face were “typical of the industry, given the speed and flexibility with which people operate”.
Writing in The Atlantic magazine, Robinson wrote: “I agree with other recently departed staff that the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough. But I believe that we need to look deeper than specific rules or new laws. We need to talk about culture.”
Referring to OpenAI’s pace of development, he wrote: “As the company sprints from one launch to the next, it is failing to achieve the level of care that I believe is needed.”
OpenAI has, however, shown signs of caution in recent weeks following the Hugging Face incident and the revelation that it has notified more than 100 organisations about rogue agent activity. This week it announced it was scrapping the release of a next-generation AI model after researchers raised safety concerns during internal testing. OpenAI has also paused training of its most advanced models.
Geoffrey Irving, who worked at OpenAI and DeepMind before becoming chief scientist of Resolution, also joined the warnings on AI on Saturday.
Writing in Time, he said: “Recent warnings about the potential destructive power of AI are understating the severity of the situation.
“I believe there’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems, and that our actions over the next two to 10 years will determine the outcome.”
Robinson’s essay also follows the resignation of Jacob Coxon, a researcher at OpenAI rival Anthropic, who quit the Claude chatbot developer last month. He warned AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade” – and was followed by Anthropic warning there was a more than 10% chance AI would wipe out humanity within the next decade. Critics of such warnings have cautioned, however, that they are unscientific because they cannot be verified or falsified.
Robinson wrote Silicon Valley lacked an awareness of “how to handle dangerous technology” and “what it means to care for people”. Warning that OpenAI had “unimpeded optimism” about solving problems as they arose, he wrote that this internal culture meant safety failures would only grow as systems become more capable.
“Imagine ‘rogue’ agents that work like teams of hackers (for example, holding hospital computer systems for ransom) but never need to sleep,” wrote Robinson.
Robinson called for two safety changes: that AI firms rely on safety expertise in other fields such as nuclear and aviation and develop “new science” that ensures powerful systems in the future are capable of being reined in when they are operating autonomously.
“Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster,” he wrote.
An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was continuing to “strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today”, while working on dealing with the risks that might be created by future AI breakthroughs.
“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” said the spokesperson.

articles.summary: Private capital checks into Europe’s booming hostel market  Financial Times3 Travel Stocks Tied To Europe’s Budget Hostel Boom  Simply Wall StreetInvestment activity puts hostels increasingly on the hospitality radar  Hospitality & Catering NewsBrookfield, Apollo back expansion in Europe’s hostel sector  Traders Union
articles.full_text:
Simply sign up to the Travel & leisure industry myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox.
The global giants of private capital are coming for Europe’s backpackers.
Over the past 18 months, investment firms including Brookfield and Apollo have made significant investments in the European hostel industry, which is growing faster than mainstream hotels.
The plan is to finance the expansion of standardised modern hostels and further professionalise an industry that has provided a cheap and cheerful refuge to travellers on a budget for more than a century.
Hostels are “the last space of the lodging sector that hasn’t really been touched [by institutional investors],” according to Andrew Heath, a vice-president at real estate adviser JLL. “People are looking and thinking: Can [hostels] be institutionalised? Can they be standardised and premiumised?”
Brookfield, which manages about $1tn in assets, acquired London-based Generator Hostels’ European business for €776mn last year.
That followed real estate private equity firm L&G Proprium’s purchase of another European chain, A&O Hostels, in 2023. A&O secured €874mn of financing from Apollo in April. Both A&O and Generator plan to double the size of their estates.
Some fear that the growth of private equity-backed “chain hostels” will undermine the charm of the historically shabby lodgings.
“What you compromise is that local, authentic atmosphere that so many travellers love,” said Evan Tzeng, founder of travel platform StayAltered, which works with independent accommodation providers.
In the 12 months to August, the number of large hostels in Europe — defined as those with capacity for more than 100 guests — grew 13 per cent to 83. While the total number remains small, the growth is outpacing that of hotels and other types of accommodation, according to figures from analytics company CoStar collated by JLL.
Lauren Okada Young, a managing director at Toronto-based Brookfield, one of the world’s largest property investors, said institutional investors were now “circling the [hostel] market and seeing that the economic model is quite profitable and attractive”.
Brookfield, she added, was drawn to the hostel sector because there was far greater scope for expansion than in the hotel market.
Generator’s “poshtels” aim to keep costs low while adding the modern design and amenities, including rooftop terraces and full-service cafés, more commonly associated with a boutique hotel.
“The sector is very fragmented so the ability to scale a platform here is interesting,” said Philipp Westermann, co-managing partner of L&G Proprium, which backed a management-led acquisition of A&O alongside StepStone Group in 2023.
Staffing costs — an increasingly significant burden for hospitality businesses — can be lower at hostels because they do not typically offer room service, while budget pricing makes them more resilient to economic turmoil, added Westermann.
Brookfield’s Generator plans to double its European estate to 30 hostels by 2030. Chief executive Xavier Mufraggi, a former boss of Club Med, said he was looking for properties that could fit a minimum of 500 beds because the model — which relies on maintaining high levels of occupancy — was only successful at “a critical size”.
Mufraggi added that Gen Z was a major growth market because they “want to travel more but they have less income than their predecessors”.
A&O, which has more than 40 hostels across Europe, is aiming to double its portfolio in the next five years. The company is opening what it said would be Europe’s largest hostel in mid-2027 after spending €40mn to convert a former office building into a 2,500-bed hostel in the heart of Berlin.
Redundant office buildings have in recent years been a source of growth for the hostel sector in Europe.
Converting large offices into hotels can be challenging because of the need to carve up a large space into individual rooms with their own plumbing and access to natural light. But hostels, with their variable dormitory sizes and less demanding clientele, are better suited to playing this “game of Tetris,” said A&O chief executive Oliver Winter.
Mufraggi said the biggest real estate opportunity for the sector was now in struggling mid-tier hotels, which can typically generate a better return for a hostel operator.
Mass market travel companies are also pushing into hostels. UK tour operator Jet2 launched its first hostel-based holiday packages in 2025 as part of an effort to reach younger and more price-sensitive customers.

articles.title: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners? - Yahoo News Singapore
articles.summary: Can Canada be the EU's answer to 'unreliable' trade partners?  Yahoo News Singapore
articles.full_text:
With tariffs, export controls and politics turning trade into a geopolitical lever, the EU seems to be shopping for partners it can count on. Canada, a like-minded economy already tied to the bloc by a free-trade agreement, is pitching itself as one.
Ahead of the EU-Canada summit at the end of October, the two sides are discussing a partnership beyond the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA).
Prime Minister Mark Carney proposed exploring an integrated market for financial services, alongside cooperation on payments, strategic minerals, energy, AI, and defence production. Nothing has been agreed on financial passports, mutual recognition of licences, or bank access.
Fabian Zuleeg, Chief Executive and Chief Economist at the European Policy Centre, says the summit must deliver more than words. "So by the time we get to the summit, we should really be concrete," he says.
A trade order under strain
The EU's problem is dependence. It relies on the US for technology and security, on Chinese supply chains for critical inputs, and on outside suppliers for energy, at a time when trade access is increasingly used as leverage.
Canada offers economic gains, Zuleeg says, in areas like financial markets and technologies CETA does not fully cover. "The more important argument is political, and it's geopolitical."
Related
The existing EU-Canada partnership is CETA, provisionally applied since 2017. It removed 98% of tariff lines immediately, rising to 99% by 2024. Trade in goods and services reached €130 billion in 2025, up 80% from €72.1 billion in 2016, according to Commission figures.
But that model has run its course. Erik van de Merel, chief economist at the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) and associate professor at the Université Libre de Bruxelles, notes that "tariffs among developed countries and between Canada and the European Union are fairly low."
The next gains lie elsewhere, "in the area of services, technology collaboration, all these sort of intangible activities that are important for future growth," he says. Negotiations on a Digital Trade Agreement began in March 2026.
What each side wants
For the EU, the appeal is security of supply. Canada says it holds deposits of more than 34 critical minerals and is a leading producer of 10 considered essential to the energy transition. Europe needs them for batteries, grids and defence.
"We are very dependent, in particular on China, at the moment," Zuleeg says. Reducing that reliance, he argues, matters less for prices than for keeping European industry running during a dispute. Cheaper energy is possible too, he adds, but not overnight.
For Ottawa, the logic is diversification. The US takes roughly seven in ten Canadian exports, while the EU was Canada's second-largest goods-trade partner in 2024 with 7.9% of its global goods trade. Canada also wants easier access to European customers and investors for its clean-energy, mining, AI, and defence firms. Canadian pension funds could co-finance mineral-processing and infrastructure projects.
Defence is already a test case. In June 2026, Canada became the first non-European country included in the EU's €150 billion SAFE defence instrument, a possible template for sector-by-sector integration.
The rule-taker question
The hardest issue is regulation. Canada wants better access to European banking, insurance, and professional services such as law, accountancy, and architecture.
Van de Merel expects the EU to ask for something in return. "The new rules that we are going to develop, to some extent, you would have to take them over," he says. If Canada wanted to set its own banking and professional rules without European oversight or harmonisation, he argues, it would have to think again because deeper market integration is a core EU goal.
Alignment, he says, is the test of whether the project works. He adds that "one has to have regulatory alignment and I think that's going to be really key and a challenge whether this is going to be a success or not." It will not be quick. The EU's single market in services remains unfinished after decades, so a newcomer seeking the same benefits faces a long catch-up.
Zuleeg is less worried about Canada becoming a mere rule-taker. Iceland follows single-market rules because it sits in the European Economic Area, he notes, but Canada would not be joining the single market. In his view, it would keep a distinct voice, for example on foreign policy. He doubts the deal would require treaty change and considers "associate membership" a misnomer. A tailored association agreement under Article 217 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU looks the more likely legal route.
Related
Practical steps are already under way. In March 2026, a joint EU-Canada committee agreed to pursue regulatory alignment on motor vehicles and conformity assessment and to widen mutual recognition in pharmaceuticals.
The politics could still bite. In Ottawa, the question is how much EU regulation Canada can accept without a vote in EU institutions. In Brussels, candidate countries undergoing lengthy reforms may ask why Canada should get privileged access. Van de Merel is also watching the UK, which could object if Canada obtains terms it never had after Brexit.
Limits and risks
The idea should not be oversold. Canada cannot replace China's role in manufacturing and mineral processing or the scale of the US economy. Mines, refineries, and ports take years to build, and the Atlantic is a logistical hurdle. Canada's exposure to Washington means a US–Canada crisis could spill into its production and investment.
Then there is CETA itself. As of mid-September 2026, ten member states, including France, Italy, Poland, Belgium and Ireland, had still not ratified it, so its investment-protection provisions are not in force. The EU is discussing an unprecedented new tier while its flagship trade deal with Canada remains only partly ratified.
Van de Merel warns that without institutions behind it, the initiative could fizzle. "Otherwise it's just an idea that is very symbolic and without any sort of political institutional consequences," he says.

articles.title: Emilia-Romagna bets on advanced manufacturing to build its space economy edge - ET Manufacturing
articles.summary: Emilia-Romagna bets on advanced manufacturing to build its space economy edge  ET Manufacturing
articles.full_text:
The Italian region aims to apply its expertise in advanced materials, aerodynamics, AI and high-performance computing to emerging space technologies.
                                    
                    
                    
                    
                                        The engineering expertise that allows companies in Emilia-Romagna to chase fractions of a second in Formula 1 and MotoGP could increasingly find applications far beyond the racetrack, from advanced materials and aerodynamics to artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.
For Michele de Pascale, President of the Emilia-Romagna Region, this crossover between the region’s industrial strengths and the space sector is at the heart of its Space Economy ambitions.
Speaking at the Beyond Exploration Expo (BEX) in Rimini, de Pascale said the conversation around the space economy should go beyond the opportunities it can create for manufacturers.
The focus, he said, should also be on how the capabilities already developed by Italy’s industrial ecosystem can help tackle some of the technological challenges of space exploration.
“We have spent much of today asking what opportunities the Space Economy can offer the manufacturing system, Emilia-Romagna, Italy and the wider European economy. That is an important question, particularly at a time when our economies need new sources of growth,” he said.
“But I would focus on the word ‘Exploration’ in the name of this event.”
From Motor Valley to orbit
De Pascale said space represents one of humanity’s major technological challenges, making engineering expertise and industrial capabilities critical to the next phase of exploration.
For Emilia-Romagna, that capability already exists across its industrial base. The region has more than 200 aerospace companies, alongside universities, research centres and high-performance computing capabilities, according to the regional government.
De Pascale highlighted the region’s motorsport ecosystem as a particularly relevant example.
“Consider what is required to gain a fraction of a second in Formula 1 or MotoGP: advanced materials, chemistry, aerodynamics, engineering and artificial intelligence,” he said. “These are not simply dual-use capabilities. They represent highly advanced engineering expertise.”
The capabilities developed in the region’s automotive and motorsport ecosystem are increasingly relevant beyond mobility, with companies applying their research, patents, and engineering expertise to opportunities emerging in the Space Economy, he said.
The crossover is already becoming part of the region’s broader aerospace strategy. Emilia-Romagna has identified advanced materials and AI as two areas where capabilities developed in Motor Valley and other industrial sectors can support aerospace applications.
Where supercomputing meets manufacturing
The second opportunity lies in combining the region’s digital capabilities with its manufacturing capabilities.
Emilia-Romagna is home to high-performance computing capabilities, including the Cineca supercomputing ecosystem, and has been building connections between research, industry and advanced computing.
For de Pascale, the opportunity is not simply to develop more computing power, but to connect that power directly with industrial production.
"This is an opportunity for us to link supercomputing with manufacturing, where we have the capability to handle large amounts of data and make something out of it," he said.
This linkage will be very significant in the future as space exploration and Earth observation satellites will produce huge amounts of data and will need advanced simulation, materials and manufacturing capabilities."
Need for concerted public and private collaboration
De Pascale identified collaboration between government, companies and research institutions as another critical ingredient.
“The Space Economy requires these three worlds to work together,” he said. That model is already embedded in Emilia-Romagna’s industrial development approach, where universities, research centres and companies work together to develop technologies and industrial capabilities.
The region has taken this approach into the space sector as well, with its aerospace ecosystem bringing together companies, four universities, research centres and the Cineca supercomputing infrastructure.
The region was also the first Italian regional administration to co-finance microgravity experiments through Axiom Mission 3 and is now exploring opportunities related to Axiom Mission 5, scheduled for 2027.
Can BEX help build the ecosystem?
For de Pascale, BEX itself is part of that industrial strategy. Unlike traditional trade fairs that typically emerge from established industrial clusters, he said BEX is using the exhibition to help create connections within an emerging sector.
“With BEX, we are doing something slightly different. We want to become a major centre of excellence in the Space Economy, so we have started building the ecosystem through the exhibition itself,” he said.
BEX, which opened at the Rimini Expo Centre on 23 September, brought space companies together with industries including manufacturing, agriculture and healthcare, with the stated aim of creating a two-way exchange between space technologies and terrestrial capabilities.
For de Pascale, the value of such an event extends beyond business matchmaking. “A trade fair is not simply a marketplace. It is a place where companies find commercial opportunities, but it is also a place for ideas, debate and reflection. It allows people to imagine the future and rethink strategies,” he said.
That makes BEX a potential platform for an industry that is still taking shape, he added. “It is not optimism without evidence. We have seen how other sectors and exhibitions in the region have developed over time,” de Pascale said.
For Emilia-Romagna, the ambition is therefore larger than simply adding another sector to its industrial portfolio. It is about taking capabilities built on the factory floor, in motorsport, in research laboratories, and in supercomputing centres and connecting them to the next generation of space technologies.
“For Emilia-Romagna, BEX is an important part of our industrial policy strategy, and, given the importance of the people and institutions involved, I believe it has significance for Italy as a whole,” he concluded.

articles.title: Nitrite-free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals - The Guardian
articles.summary: Nitrite-free bacon sales boom in UK amid fears over curing chemicals  The GuardianTesco launches nitrite-free bacon and ham range using 100 percent British pork  New FoodWaitrose expands nitrite-free range as demand surges by 34%  Retail BulletinWaitrose Expands Nitrite-Free Meat Range  KamCity
articles.full_text:
Bacon has long been a favourite of carnivores, but there is growing consumer concern about the health risks posed by nitrites, chemicals used to cure meats.
While many experts argue there is no evidence processed meat made without nitrites is safer, retailers have responded to consumer concerns by offering “nitrite-free” products to meet demand.
Denhay, the Devon hand- dry-cured bacon specialist, has launched two new back bacon lines in 570 Tesco stores from 21 September – Made Without Nitrites Smoked Back Bacon and Made Without Nitrites Unsmoked Back Bacon (both 200g), both priced at £4.
Waitrose has doubled its Made Without Nitrites range in the past year, with sales up more than 34%. Sales of its British roast and honey roast hams have risen more than 70% since launching in May, and its unsmoked back bacon is up 22%.
Data from Worldpanel by Numerator shows nitrite-free bacon growing steadily while conventional bacon declines, and its share of the fresh bacon category has risen steadily from a small base. In the 52 weeks to 6 September 2026, nitrite-free spend reached £34.8m (up 11.4% year on year) and volumes were up to 2.2m kg (up 8.0%), while spend and volume for conventional bacon was 9.2% and 4.9%, respectively.
Emer Lowry, a nutritionist at Waitrose, said: “As our customers pay closer attention to on-pack ingredient lists, providing options without added nitrites gives shoppers more choice without compromising on flavour and taste.”
Marlene Godwin, the managing director of Denhay, said the move was prompted by retailers and shoppers rather than the producer. “We definitely don’t want to be telling people what to eat. This is about giving bacon lovers choice, not replacement. Retailers were saying customers want this, can you provide it?
She added: “I can’t speak for shoppers, but I think health consciousness is driving it, and consumers are more interested. One of the things people said to me was, why not convert everything? Our customers still love traditional cure, but we’re offering another choice.”
Sodium and potassium nitrates and nitrites are chemicals that are often used to preserve or “cure” meat.
Nitrates, which contain one nitrogen and three oxygens atoms, can be converted by bacteria into nitrites, which contain one nitrogen and two oxygen atoms.
Nitrites help to prevent the growth of microbes, including harmful bacteria, and can enhance the flavour and pink colour of meat products.
People do not consume these chemicals only through eating meat – nitrates are also provided by vegetables, in particular leafy greens.
The Food Standards Agency (FSA) says the key difference is that when nitrates or nitrites are consumed as part of protein-rich foods such as meat, they are converted into chemicals known as nitrosamines, which are thought to be harmful to health.
“Vegetables provide nitrates alongside beneficial nutrients such as vitamin C, polyphenols and fibre. These nutrients help to reduce the formation of harmful nitrosamines,” the FSA adds
The World Health Organization’s cancer agency classes processed meat as a group 1 carcinogen, the same category as tobacco, though the known link between processed meat and cancer cannot be directly attributed to nitrites.
Research suggests eating about 50g of processed meat a day, roughly two rashers of bacon, is linked to a 16% higher relative risk of colorectal cancer.
The FSA says no single component of processed meat has been identified as the cause, and there is no definitive evidence that nitrites directly cause cancer.
The FSA also says there is no evidence that processed meats made without nitrate or nitrite additives are safer. It adds that removing them can create food safety challenges, because they help prevent the growth of dangerous bacteria and must be replaced by other methods of preservation.
Gabriela Peacock, a nutritionist and founder of GP Nutrition, said: “People are much more interested in what is actually in their food now. They are turning packets over, reading ingredient lists and looking for products that feel a little less processed. If someone enjoys bacon or ham but sees an option made without added nitrates, it can feel like a very easy, positive swap, without having to change the way they eat completely.”
Peacock said nitrite-free products are often more expensive. “That may be because they are made by smaller producers, use different curing methods or have a shorter shelf life. They may also use higher-welfare meat or more expensive ingredients. Sometimes, of course, you are paying for the premium positioning and packaging too,” she said.
She added: “The most expensive option is not automatically the healthiest, just as ‘nitrate-free’ does not give a product a magic health halo. Nitrates and nitrites help to preserve meat and control harmful bacteria, and the Food Standards Agency says there is currently no evidence that processed meat made without them is safer.”

articles.title: Ukraine war fatigue fuels defense-spending downgrade plan in Italy - Defense News
articles.summary: Ukraine war fatigue fuels defense-spending downgrade plan in Italy  Defense News
articles.full_text:
ROME — Italian military planners risk losing out on €8 billion ($9 billion) in funding as government and opposition parties seek to cut both defense spending and support for Ukraine.
The plans to limit spending emerged this week as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni continues to be squeezed between NATO spending targets and voter opposition to spending tax payers’ cash on arms not hospitals.
The possible €8 billion shortfall is tied up with Italy’s hot-and-cold approach to a European Union scheme to allow states to exempt a quantity of defense spending from their calculations of annual deficit spending over a number of years.
The so-called National Escape Clause would allow EU states to rearm while not breaking EU deficit rules.
After Meloni’s government promoted the scheme, it then appeared less enthusiastic when the EU finally approved it before Meloni announced this year she would use the extra cash not only for defense but also to cover Italy’s soaring fuel costs.
That was due to generate a defense windfall of between €21 billion and €22 billion thanks to NEC. But the calculation changed on Thursday at a Cabinet meeting when deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini succeeded in pushing the amount down to around €14 billion, a drop of up to €8 billion.
“It’s yet to be made definite but the reduction was agreed,” a government source told Defense News.
Salvini leads the League party which is part of Meloni’s governing coalition and is battling defense spending hikes, opposing sending military support to Ukraine and wants a deal with Moscow to end the conflict in the country.
That contrasts with Meloni’s firm backing for Kyiv and support for Europe’s hardline opposition to Moscow, but she is in a minority in Italian politics. To her right, a new challenger Roberto Vannacci is calling for an end to sanctions on Russia, while among Italy’s left-wing opposition parties, the Five Star party has blamed the Ukraine conflict on a “war mongering Europe.”
A poll of Five Star’s members this month found over 90% opposed European rearmament and believed sending arms to Ukraine was to blame for prolonging the war.
Despite a groundswell of opposition to defense spending in Italy, Meloni has meanwhile committed to NATO’s spending target of 5% of GDP, and she has claimed Italy has reached 2.8% this year, including spending on domestic security.
But details are scant: this year’s budget breakdown has yet to be published.
Meanwhile, Rome said in August it would request €8 billion euros in cheap loans from the European Union’s SAFE defense funding program, down from its original intention to ask for €14.9 billion euros in loans.
In a parliamentary hearing on Sept. 23, the CEO of Italian defense giant Leonardo said he was a big fan of SAFE loans, since they guaranteed cash for defense programs with few complications.
“I believe SAFE is the first, real useful measure that Europe has come up with,” said Lorenzo Mariani.
“The money has never been much and it’s been complicated. Now SAFE is moving a lot of money and using a system which we believe is not complex like other European schemes have been,” he added.
“Portugal is buying FREMM frigates built by Leonardo and Fincantieri thanks to SAFE funds,” he said.
Mariani said he had talked up the virtues of SAFE loans to the Meloni government.
“SAFE is very positive. The use of it does not depend on me. I have made proposals which I hope are accepted by the government,” he said.
One analyst said Rome needed to make up its mind about spending.
“The government needs to take important decisions about NEC and SAFE loans which were granted to all member states after years of requests by Italian governments,” said Alessandro Marrone, who heads the Defence Security and Space Programme at Rome think tank IAI.
“The government should have implemented its decision by now to enable better planning by the Italian defense ministry. It’s urgent. This is not just about NATO targets but about filling gaps left in Europe next year by U.S. pull-outs and now following through on Italy’s desire to send naval vessels to defend the Red Sea.”
Tom Kington is the Italy correspondent for Defense News.

articles.title: Eurozone Inflation Hits 3-Year High of 3.8% Last Month - news.sbs.co.kr
articles.summary: Eurozone Inflation Hits 3-Year High of 3.8% Last Month  news.sbs.co.kr
articles.full_text:
Inflation in the eurozone (the 21 countries using the euro) surged to a three-year high last month, driven by soaring energy prices.
According to Eurostat, the European Union's statistical office, on the 2nd local time, the eurozone's consumer price index for September was provisionally estimated to have risen 3.8% from a year earlier.
This marks the largest increase in three years since September 2023 (4.3%).
The growth rate widened significantly compared to 3.2% in August, and slightly exceeded the 3.7% forecast by experts compiled by Bloomberg.
Energy prices jumped 18.8% year-on-year, pulling up the overall inflation rate.
As the Middle East war, which has continued for over half a year, and the prolonged blockade of the Strait of Hormuz persisted, the rate easily surpassed the previous month's increase of 14.3%.
Service sector inflation also rose 3.2%, expanding from the previous month's 3.0%, while core inflation—which excludes volatile items such as energy, food, and alcohol—also edged up slightly from 2.4% in August to 2.5% last month.
As inflation continues to significantly exceed the 2% target, the possibility of the European Central Bank (ECB) implementing additional interest rate hikes at its monetary policy meeting this month is growing, AFP reported.
To curb soaring inflation, the ECB raised interest rates in June for the first time since 2023, followed by another rate hike last month.

Euro-area inflation quickened more than expected to the highest in three years, bolstering expectations that the European Central Bank will lift interest rates further.
Consumer prices rose 3.8% from a year ago in September, up from 3.2% the previous month, Eurostat said on Friday. That’s the highest since September 2023 and slightly above the 3.7% median estimate in a Bloomberg survey.
Core inflation — excluding volatile items like energy, which has driven the latest bout of price pressure — rose to 2.5% as anticipated. The services gauge advanced to 3.2%.
Read More
Europe is in the midst of a renewed inflation upswing as the failure to end the Iran war jolts oil and natural gas markets higher again. Prices jumped more than anticipated in each of the euro area’s four largest members, reaching as high as 5% in Spain.
The 21-nation economy has held up well, particularly after the ECB hiked borrowing costs twice. But governments, whose finances were already stretched, are struggling to support households and firms amid a global bond sell-off.
ECB officials want to prevent the energy shock from becoming embedded in the economy through things like big wage demands and higher company selling prices. They’re expected to raise interest rates at least twice more, though bets on a move this month are fading.
President Christine Lagarde kicked off remarks from key policymakers this week suggesting there’s no rush to tighten monetary policy further, saying higher yields will curb economic expansion and limit the transfer of the energy shock to broader prices.
Executive board member Isabel Schnabel struck a similar note by saying a “clearer picture” of the inflation picture will emerge over the coming months.
Despite its resilience to date, doubts are building over the economy’s ability to withstand the latest onslaught in prices. Spurred by rising public outrage, countries like Germany have cut fuel taxes to ease soaring prices at the pump.
The ECB worries, however, that such untargeted measures could make the overall inflation problem even worse.
There are other signs, too, that worse is to come. A monthly poll by the European Commission found firms’ selling-price expectations held above long-term averages in all sectors, while consumers’ inflation expectations for the next 12 months rose "noticeably".

The investment focuses on components embedded in fighter aircraft, radars and satellites. These chips handle functions including signal processing and control logic, enabling systems to detect, process and respond to threats.
Northrop Grumman manufactures and procures millions of microchips in the United States each year. It operates three government-accredited manufacturing facilities across Maryland, California and Florida and plans to expand domestic capabilities and partnerships.
“With our deep end-to-end knowledge and manufacturing capabilities, we can deliver the right chip, with the right capability to the right mission, every time,” said Robert Mendoza, operations manager at the company’s Redondo Beach, California, microelectronics facility. “With our extensive background working with these technologies, we have perfected ways to add a broad range of functions to support our nation’s military and commercial needs.”
Advanced packaging reduces size and power requirements
Alongside chip fabrication, Northrop Grumman provides advanced packaging that combines chips with different properties and functions into a single solution. Three-dimensional stacking allows those components to deliver more functionality while occupying less space and consuming less power.
“These 3-dimensional chip-stacking methods allow our products to do more, faster – while taking up less space and using less power,” said Brittany Battaglia, Advanced Packaging Program Manager. “It’s critical technology.”
The company said it operates one of the few U.S.-based advanced packaging facilities. According to Northrop Grumman, 98% of American chipmakers must source those services internationally.
Manufacturing draws on more than 800 materials
Chip production begins with semiconductor wafers, typically made from silicon or compounds such as gallium arsenide and indium phosphide. Northrop Grumman said it has access to more than 800 materials to support its microelectronics work.
Wafers undergo repeated cycles of deposition, photolithography and etching to create the required devices. Once fabrication and testing are complete, individual chips are separated using diamond saw blades or lasers.
“Fabricating wafers is like baking a tiered cake — each layer uses different recipes and ingredients, and variables like temperature and time can affect the texture, taste, or look of the cake,” said Vicky Zheng, a process integration engineer at the company’s Baltimore facility. Northrop Grumman said its engineers continue to refine these processes and develop new manufacturing approaches.
Domestic capacity addresses supply-chain exposure
The company cited the semiconductor industry’s dependence on Taiwan and threats from China as reasons to expand U.S. production. It said additional domestic capacity would benefit Northrop Grumman programs and external defense and commercial customers.
The expansion is expected to support employment for thousands of Americans and contribute to local economies. Northrop Grumman said its domestic manufacturing investment also supports innovation and the development of long-term semiconductor expertise.

articles.full_text:
On Friday, October 2, eurozone inflation for September once again became the central factor driving pricing in euro‑denominated assets. The latest flash estimate shows headline inflation rising to 3.8% year on year, up from 3.2% in August, while core inflation edged up from 2.4% to 2.5%. The euro/dollar exchange rate is currently hovering around 1.124, remaining near its lows since late September.
Inflation Surge: Energy Sets the Pace, Core Inflation Determines Sustainability
The most notable development in Europe in September was not a surge in core inflation, but rather a widening of the year-on-year increase in the energy component, which rose from 14.3% to 18.8%, directly pushing overall inflation up by 0.6 percentage points. Meanwhile, service‑sector inflation edged up from 3.0% to 3.2%, and the food component also showed signs of rebounding. The growing gap between headline and core inflation suggests that current price pressures remain strongly energy‑driven; however, the renewed acceleration in service prices indicates that cost pass‑through is no longer confined to the energy sector.
For the market, the headline reading of 3.8% first affects the short-term inflation risk premium, while the core reading of 2.5% determines policymakers' sensitivity to second-round effects. What truly matters is not how high headline inflation is in any given month, but whether energy costs can persistently feed through to wages, service prices, and non‑energy goods. If this transmission intensifies, energy shocks will gradually shift from relative price adjustments to broader inflationary stickiness.
ECB: Following the rate hike, the policy‑making framework places greater emphasis on transmission.
In September, the European Central Bank raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points, bringing the deposit facility rate, the main refinancing rate, and the marginal lending rate to 2.50%, 2.65%, and 2.90%, respectively. According to the September baseline projections, headline inflation is expected to average 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028, while core inflation is projected at 2.5%, 2.6%, and 2.3%, respectively. This suggests that even as the direct impact of energy prices gradually wanes, underlying price pressures may still ease only gradually.
On September 30, Sabine Lautenschläger, a member of the European Central Bank's Executive Board, stated that monetary policy "cannot wait until spillover effects and second-round effects have fully materialized before taking action." The policy implication is clear: the duration of the energy shock, the extent to which firms pass on cost increases, wage‑price feedback, and long-term inflation expectations have all become more important than the headline inflation figure alone. At the same time, rising long-term yields themselves tighten financial conditions, meaning that monetary policy must contend with a combination of inflationary pressures and tightening financial conditions.
Euro/Dollar: The inflation‑spread rationale has been offset by financial conditions.
The euro–dollar exchange rate is currently around 1.124, compared with roughly 1.133 on September 30, reflecting a marked increase in short-term volatility. On the inflation front, higher readings in the eurozone are likely to heighten market attention to the European Central Bank's commitment to maintaining a restrictive policy stance. However, rising energy prices also erode real incomes, weigh on terms of trade, and push up bond yields, thereby raising financing costs; as a result, exchange-rate movements cannot be fully explained by nominal interest-rate expectations alone.
On the other hand, in September, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%, and a significant gap in policy rates between Europe and the United States persists. For the euro–dollar exchange rate, a more informative analytical framework involves disaggregating the euro–U.S. interest-rate spread, energy shocks, and risk premiums, rather than attributing the 3.8% inflation figure directly to a single exchange-rate outcome.
Technological Structure: Coexistence of Vulnerability and Volatile Expansion
The daily chart shows that prices remain below the Bollinger Middle Band and are approaching the lower band, with the Bollinger Band width indicating a marked increase in price dispersion compared to the prior period. On the MACD, the DIF stands at -0.0077 and the DEA at -0.0052; both lines are below the zero axis, and the negative histogram bars continue to expand. Meanwhile, the Bollinger Middle Band is trending downward, reflecting a sustained shift in the price center of gravity over the past few weeks.
These indicators capture the strength of past trends, volatility, and momentum. During periods of high event density, greater informational value lies in observing whether price volatility, yield curve spreads, and momentum metrics exhibit synchronized shifts following the release of inflation data. When these three factors diverge, the resulting market implications are often more complex than those suggested by any single technical indicator.
Frequently Asked Questions
Question 1: Why has headline inflation risen to 3.8%, while core inflation remains at only 2.5%?
Answer: This round of inflationary pressure is largely driven by the energy sector, with energy prices rising 18.8% year-on-year in September—significantly outpacing other components such as services. Core measures exclude highly volatile items like energy, resulting in a much more modest increase; this distinction is key to assessing whether the shock is spreading across the broader price structure.
Question 2: Does inflation exceeding expectations necessarily mean the euro will strengthen?
Answer: They are not equivalent. Higher inflation will alter the European Central Bank's interest-rate expectations, but energy costs will also erode real incomes, raise financing costs, and weigh on growth prospects. Ultimately, the exchange rate reflects a composite of the U.S.-Eurozone yield spread, financial conditions, and risk premiums.

articles.title: Iran War Pushes Eurozone Inflation to 3.8 Percent - trendingtopics.eu
articles.summary: Iran War Pushes Eurozone Inflation to 3.8 Percent  trendingtopics.eu
articles.full_text:
The war in the Persian Gulf is now hitting supermarket checkouts and gas pumps. Inflation in the euro area rose to 3.8 percent in September, up from 3.2 percent in August, according to a flash estimate just released by the E.U. statistics office Eurostat. It is the highest reading in three years; inflation was last this high in the fall of 2023. Economists had on average expected a slightly smaller increase. The rate is now almost double the European Central Bank’s 2 percent target.
Energy Is the Main Driver
Energy accounts for nearly half of the increase. Energy prices were 18.8 percent higher in September than a year earlier, compared with 14.3 percent in August. The reason is the war between the United States and Iran, which has been pushing up oil prices for months. Before the war, about a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed through the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has since been severely restricted. In September, Brent crude rose more than 14 percent to around $103 (about 88 euros) a barrel. Most recently, President Trump rejected a proposal from Tehran to reopen the strait, sending prices higher still.
“It is above all the massive increases in energy prices that drove inflation to its highest level since the fall of 2023,” said Jörg Krämer, chief economist at Commerzbank, as the German newspaper Rhein-Zeitung reported. Food prices also climbed: Unprocessed food rose 4.0 percent, after 2.7 percent the month before. Services prices increased 3.2 percent.
The differences between eurozone countries are large:
- Lithuania: 6.1 percent, the highest rate in the eurozone
- Spain: 5.0 percent
- Italy: 4.1 percent, up from 3.2 percent in August
- France: 3.4 percent
- Germany: 3.3 percent
In Austria, inflation rose to 3.6 percent from 3.2 percent in August, Statistics Austria said in its flash estimate. Energy cost 14.5 percent more than a year earlier. The increase of 0.4 percentage points was entirely due to higher prices for fuel and heating oil, said Manuela Lenk, the agency’s director general.
The E.C.B. Is Under Pressure
For monetary policy, the situation is tricky. The E.C.B. has already raised its deposit rate twice this year, most recently in September by 0.25 percentage points to 2.5 percent. Trending Topics reported on the jump in inflation in August ahead of that move. Many economists now expect another increase. “An E.C.B. rate hike in December is as good as set in stone,” said Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank. A move as early as October is seen as possible if energy prices keep rising.
There are also arguments against tightening quickly. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, rose only slightly, from 2.4 to 2.5 percent. That suggests the energy shock has so far barely spilled over into other prices. The E.C.B. also sees no second-round effects in wages yet: Wages “do not show a material response to the energy shock at this stage,” E.C.B. President Christine Lagarde said after the September rate decision. Higher interest rates also do nothing to increase the supply of oil, but they do slow an economy that contracted in the first quarter.
What It Means for Households and Businesses
For consumers, high inflation means above all that filling up the car and heating the home are getting much more expensive, just as the heating season begins. Several governments are trying to counter this. Germany is cutting its fuel tax by about 17 cents per liter from October through the end of the year. Overall, however, government support across the eurozone has so far been modest, at about 0.1 percent of economic output.
Rising interest rates also make loans more expensive. That affects homeowners with variable-rate mortgages as well as companies that want to invest. Start-ups face a tougher environment, too, because investors find safe assets more attractive again when rates are higher. On top of that, borrowing costs for governments are rising: Yields on French government bonds are at their highest level in decades.
What happens next depends above all on the price of oil, and therefore on the course of the Iran war. A reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would quickly ease energy prices, while further escalation would push inflation even higher.

By Sudeshna Ghoshal
Oct 2 (Reuters) – European stocks rebounded on Friday after a sharp selloff driven by a bond market rout, while investors parsed inflation data for fresh clues on monetary policy.
The pan-European STOXX 600 rose 0.6% to 630.47 points by 1005 GMT, after touching its lowest in more than three months on Thursday.
Data showed euro zone inflation surged more than expected in September and is likely to rise further in the coming months, keeping pressure on the European Central Bank to raise interest rates again.
“Higher interest rates combined with elevated inflation are a negative for equities, but whether equity markets will react badly depends on how long investors feel the problem will last,” said Michael Field, chief equity strategist at Morningstar.
The ECB lifted interest rates last month, and traders are currently pricing in 81.8% chances of a rate hike in December, LSEG data showed.
Equities have been battered in recent weeks as global government bond yields surged to multi-year highs, leaving investors averse to risk assets.
European banking stocks dipped 0.3% and were on track for their worst week since April, hurt by concerns about higher interest rates denting the economy.
Germany’s Commerzbank dropped 1.4% after RBC downgraded the stock to “sector perform” from “outperform”.
France presented its 2027 budget on Thursday, seeking to enact unpopular belt-tightening measures aimed at reducing the deficit and reassuring bond markets ahead of next year’s presidential election.
Late last month, France’s 10-year borrowing costs reached the highest since the global financial crisis in 2008.
“The French election and the French big fiscal problem is going to weigh on sentiment,” said Ricardo Castillo, head of investments at Mirabaud Group.
Focus is on US nonfarm payrolls data expected around 1230 GMT, with forecasts estimating a gain of 90,000 jobs in September. A hot print could revive bets on a second rate hike from the Federal Reserve this month. Markets see a 25% change of a hike after two top policymakers said this week they wanted more data before deciding what to do next.
In Europe, technology shares led sectoral gains, up 2.1%, boosted by advances in ASM International NV and ASML.
Puma rose 1.6%, reversing course after slipping earlier. US peer Nike projected a surprisingly steep drop in full-year revenue as it continues to grapple with weak demand in China and heightened competition.
Shares in Julius Baer rose 2.3% after the Swiss bank announced a share buyback programme of up to 600 million Swiss francs ($724 million).

articles.summary: Eurozone inflation hits three-year high of 3.8%  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Eurozone inflation shot up to a three-year high of 3.8 per cent in September after the escalating conflict in the Middle East triggered a resurgence in oil and gas prices.
The reading published by Eurostat on Friday was up from 3.2 per cent in August and higher than economists’ forecast of 3.6 per cent in a Reuters poll. In all four of the Eurozone’s largest economies, inflation rose at a faster pace than expected, with Spain reporting an annual rate of 5 per cent.
The increase was driven by fuel prices. Energy inflation jumped to 18.8 per cent from 14.3 per cent in August, reaching the highest level since January 2023 during the energy price crisis triggered by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine the previous year.
“Over the coming months, the currently high oil price could push headline inflation towards 4 per cent,” warned Ulrike Kastens, economist at asset manager DWS. But she added that a “similarly sharp rise” in core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was not on the cards as “wage growth is likely to remain subdued”.
Rising inflation and concerns over the sustainability of public finances in more indebted countries such as France have triggered a surge in Eurozone borrowing costs.
That pushed up yields of French 10-year government bonds as much as 0.1 percentage points to 4.96 per cent on Thursday, their highest level since 2002. They have since come back down to 4.87 per cent.
September marked the seventh consecutive month that inflation in the 21-country bloc was above the European Central Bank’s medium-term 2 per cent target.
Annual core inflation rose 0.1 percentage points in September to 2.5 per cent. The closely watched figure for services inflation rose to 3.2 per cent from 3 per cent in August. The figure, a gauge of domestic price pressures, has remained well above the ECB’s target for more than three years.
The ECB was the first central bank in the G7 to respond to the Middle East energy shock, increasing borrowing costs by a quarter-point in June and again in September.
Traders are betting that policymakers will respond by raising interest rates by another quarter point to 2.75 per cent by the end of the year. They are attributing a roughly 25 per cent chance to a quarter-point rate rise being announced at the next ECB meeting later this month and about an 85 per cent probability that the move comes at December’s meeting, according to levels implied by swaps contracts.
Top ECB official Isabel Schnabel said this week that rate-setters must act pre-emptively to stop high energy prices from feeding into broader prices and wages.
Lee Hardman, senior currency analyst at MUFG, said there was “limited evidence” so far of high energy prices spilling into the wider economy, noting that this “and tightening financial conditions should keep the ECB on hold until December”.
Headline inflation “is clearly hot” but core inflation, at 2.5 per cent, “indicates again no evidence of second-round effects”, said Francesco Pesole, FX strategist at ING, although he added that the jump in the headline number obviously “isn’t great news given all that’s going on in France”.
The euro was stable following the data, up 0.2 per cent against the US dollar by late afternoon in London at $1.126.
